lof.name: Left of Field Golf
lof.desc: Nick Ilias started Left of Field in his brother’s old bedroom in 2022, working from surf and skate silhouettes rather than golf ones — “our mission isn’t to create products that scream ‘golf’.” Every collection takes its name from a stretch of Australian coast: Elements for Barnbougle in Tasmania, SOUTH for the Mornington Peninsula, RNP for Royal National Park below Sydney. The sustainability page commits to recycled-PET yarn, which almost nobody this size does.
lof.old: The one that opened the door for most of the others. Nick Ilias started it in his brother’s old bedroom in 2022, and the brief was never golf clothing: it was surf and skate silhouettes that happened to work on a course. In his words, “our mission isn’t to create products that scream ‘golf’.” Every collection is named for a stretch of Australian coast — Elements for Barnbougle in Tasmania, SOUTH for the Mornington Peninsula, RNP for Royal National Park below Sydney. They also publish a sustainability page committing to recycled-PET yarn, which almost nobody at this size does.

walker.name: Walker Golf Things
walker.desc: Jack Fardell runs Walker out of the Gold Coast, a professional skateboarder whose father named him after Jack Nicklaus — “I didn’t really have a choice but to play golf.” The collaborations come constantly: Evan Mock’s Wahine, Coopers the brewery, Shortees the floodlit Sydney par-three. Riding for adidas Skateboarding since 2015 is how a small label ended up with an adidas Golf capsule in 2024, built around a co-designed MC-Z Traxion shoe.
walker.old: Founded by Jack Fardell, a professional skateboarder whose father named him after Jack Nicklaus — “I didn’t really have a choice but to play golf.” He has ridden for adidas Skateboarding since 2015, which is how a small Gold Coast label ended up with an adidas Golf capsule in 2024, built around a co-designed MC-Z Traxion shoe. The most prolific brand here by a distance, and the most collaborative — Evan Mock’s Wahine, Coopers the brewery, and Shortees, the floodlit Sydney par-three.

penta.name: Penta Golf
penta.desc: Penta is three friends who met working at a creative print magazine and a youth-culture agency, and who have never put their names on the site. The Etiquette Pants and the PXB line with Barnaby’s read like a magazine art department made golf clothes. Asked where they play, they were specific: “anywhere on the Northern Beaches… but Warringah Golf Club is our local.” The last drop was December 2025, so the range is stocked but static.
penta.old: Three friends who met working at a creative print magazine and a youth-culture agency, and who have never put their names on the site. It shows in the product — the Etiquette Pants and the PXB line with Barnaby’s read like a magazine art department made golf clothes. Asked where they play, the answer was refreshingly specific: “anywhere on the Northern Beaches… but Warringah Golf Club is our local. Shout out to Rob and Greg at the Pro Shop.” One flag: their last drop was December 2025, so the range is stocked but static.

midiron.name: Midiron
midiron.desc: Midiron has made nine products in eight months and named nobody behind them. Most of it is shot at night under a hard flash on a floodlit par-three, and every second product page signs off “Golf Apparel Research approved” — Golf Apparel Research being their own house name. The best thing they have made is a reworked vintage Titleist cap, sold as three one-offs, with an unsigned story about a grandad’s hand-me-down underneath it.
midiron.old: The newest and smallest, and the one that names nobody at all. Nine products in eight months, most of it shot at night under a hard flash on a floodlit par-three. Every second product page signs off “Golf Apparel Research approved,” which reads like an endorsement until you realise Golf Apparel Research is their own house name. The best thing they have made is a reworked vintage Titleist cap, sold as three one-offs, with an unsigned story about a grandad’s hand-me-down underneath it.

birds.name: Birds of Condor
birds.desc: Birds of Condor began with Frankie Kimpton sneaking out of his booking-agent job at Mushroom Records to hit balls at Albert Park in black jeans and a Guns N’ Roses shirt — “I think it was 20 bucks for a bucket of balls and a beer.” The first drop was ten hats. Several hundred products and a Culture Kings stockist list later, the Byron Bay flagship holds a restored 1980s buggy from Sanctuary Cove.
birds.old: The most established brand on this list and the one you have probably already seen. Frankie Kimpton was a booking agent at Mushroom Records, sneaking out at lunch to hit balls at Albert Park — “I think it was 20 bucks for a bucket of balls and a beer” — in black jeans and a Guns N’ Roses shirt. The first drop was ten hats. It is now several hundred products, a Culture Kings stockist list, and a Byron Bay flagship containing a restored 1980s buggy from Sanctuary Cove.

okka.name: Okka Golf
okka.desc: One person screen-prints everything Okka sells, in Perth, and keeps it that way on purpose. The answer to wholesale, posted on their own site, is “no bueno amigo. not something i do. i’m extremely protective of the relationship i have with frens of OKKA.” Every piece is shot the same way on the same backdrop, like a lookbook made by someone who only owns one light.
okka.old: Screen-printed by one person in Perth, and militantly kept that way. Asked about wholesale, the answer on their own site is “no bueno amigo. not something i do. i’m extremely protective of the relationship i have with frens of OKKA.” The stated aim is the opposite of a pitch deck: not “changing the game,” not a vanity project. The photography is the giveaway — every piece shot the same way on the same backdrop, like a lookbook made by someone who only owns one light.

grayhaast.name: Gray + Haast
grayhaast.desc: Gray is the founder’s surname and Haast is for the Haast’s eagle, the largest eagle known to have existed, which makes the name a joke about the score every golfer chases and never makes. The clothing is the most conventionally handsome of the Australian brands, and the Peninsula long-sleeve polo and the Performance Shell are the two to start with. Noosa Golf Co stocks them, and new product lands regularly.
grayhaast.old: The most conventionally handsome clothing here, and the best name. Gray is the founder’s surname; Haast is for the Haast’s eagle, the largest eagle known to have existed and a decent joke about the score every golfer is chasing and never makes. The Peninsula long-sleeve polo and the Performance Shell are the pieces to start with. Stocked at Noosa Golf Co, and dropping regularly — there was new product on the site the day we wrote this.

found.name: Found Golf
found.desc: Lance Peach and Ellen Keillar have run Found since 2022, and thirty-five of their fifty-eight products are art rather than apparel — paintings, sculpture, a bench listed at nearly six thousand dollars. The clothing that does exist is made where possible with boutique ateliers in Cape Town, with the ex-AFL player Dale Thomas as creative partner. They also sell golf tees in a reusable cigarette box, which tells you the register.
found.old: Barely a clothing brand. Lance Peach and Ellen Keillar have been running it since 2022, and thirty-five of their fifty-eight products are art rather than apparel — paintings, sculpture, a bench listed at nearly six thousand dollars. The clothing that does exist is made, where possible, with boutique ateliers in Cape Town. Ex-AFL player Dale Thomas is their creative partner. They also sell golf tees in a reusable cigarette box, which tells you the register.

mackem.name: Mackem Golf
mackem.desc: Mackem makes wool-blend headcovers and waxed-canvas pouches, all sewn in-house in the Perth hills, with a real shop on Haynes Street you can walk into. The bespoke work has turned football shirts, wedding suits and boardshorts into covers, and one set came from a family tartan embroidered with the initials of a customer’s late father. Adam is blunt about scaling: “we’re not Amazon Prime and never want to be.”
mackem.old: Wool-blend headcovers and waxed-canvas pouches, all sewn in-house in the Perth hills, with a real shop on Haynes Street you can walk into. Their bespoke work has turned football shirts, wedding suits and boardshorts into covers. The one Adam tells is a set made from a family tartan and embroidered with the initials of a customer’s late father: “he wished they had spent more time together on the golf course. That really got me.” On scaling up, he is blunt — “we’re not Amazon Prime and never want to be.”

bigdog.name: Big Dog Golf Co.
bigdog.desc: Mark Calder started Big Dog on a dining table in a Brunswick apartment in 2019, having noticed that The Big Dog® was common shorthand for the driver and that nobody had trademarked it. The leather covers now sit in the pro shops at Royal Melbourne, Barnbougle, Royal Adelaide, Peninsula Kingswood and Cape Wickham, plus Tara Iti and Te Arai Links across the Tasman. If you are building an Australian trip, this is the souvenir.
bigdog.old: Mark Calder started this on a dining table in a Brunswick apartment in 2019 after noticing something nobody had bothered to do. In his words: “I couldn’t believe — The Big Dog® — is commonly used when referring to the driver, so I thought, why not trademark it and see what we can do?” The leather covers are now in the pro shops at Royal Melbourne, Barnbougle, Royal Adelaide, NSW, Victoria, Peninsula Kingswood and Cape Wickham, plus Tara Iti and Te Arai Links across the Tasman. If you are building an Australian trip, this is the souvenir.

#11.name: Random Golf Club — The Long Way Round
#11.desc: Random Golf Club takes fourteen players through Kingston Heath, Victoria, Peninsula Kingswood North, both Nationals and St Andrews Beach, opening at Royal Park, the Melbourne public course where the first meetup happened. Al and Erik Anders Lang drive the vans themselves, promising “a smaller group and no fixed leash.” Golf, lodging, transport and breakfast are in; airfare and caddies are not. It finishes with 36 holes of matchplay for the Random Cup.
#11.old: The one trip on this page built for the people who read this site, and the only community-led Australia trip that exists. Fourteen players, and an itinerary that opens at Royal Park — the Melbourne public course where the first Random Golf Club meetup happened — before getting into Kingston Heath, Victoria, Peninsula Kingswood North, both Nationals and St Andrews Beach. Al and Erik Anders Lang drive the vans themselves, which is the whole pitch: “a smaller group and no fixed leash, so if someone fancies a dip in the sea after golf… we go and have one.” Golf, lodging, transport and breakfast are in; airfare, caddies and trolleys are not. Australians can buy a stripped-back local ticket at US$4,995. It closes with 36 holes of matchplay for the Random Cup, and if you are not ready to go home it runs straight into their Japan Major.

#12.name: Jet Set Golf — The Big 5
#12.desc: Air Adventure Australia has flown out of regional Victoria since 1977, and the Big 5 puts you in a Pilatus PC-12 that lands at the course — “as little as 90 minutes from take-off to tee-off.” That is the clean answer to King Island, where no passenger ferry crosses Bass Strait. Five days covers Barnbougle Dunes, Lost Farm, Seven Mile Beach, Cape Wickham and Ocean Dunes, with a A$285 surcharge for international players.
#12.old: A Pilatus PC-12 that lands at the golf course. Air Adventure Australia has been flying out of regional Victoria since 1977 and their own pitch is “as little as 90 minutes from take-off to tee-off” — which is the only clean answer to the King Island problem, because there is no passenger ferry across Bass Strait and the commercial flights are small. Five days covers Barnbougle Dunes, Lost Farm, Seven Mile Beach, Cape Wickham and Ocean Dunes, with a night on site at Cape Wickham. Two footnotes: there is a A$285 green fee and accommodation surcharge across the five courses for international players, and the advertised rate is flagged as expiring at the end of August 2026, so treat the number as indicative.

1.label: Apparel · eight brands
1.text: Australia’s independent golf scene got good fast, and in a specific way: surf and skate silhouettes, coastal names, and no interest in looking like a pro shop. All eight ship internationally, and most price in Australian dollars.
1.old: Australia’s independent golf scene got good fast, and it got good in a specific way — surf and skate silhouettes, coastal names, and almost no interest in looking like a pro shop. Most price in Australian dollars, which is quietly good news for an American — though note that Left of Field runs a US storefront in dollars and Birds of Condor a New Zealand one, so what you see may already be converted. All eight ship internationally.

2.label: Leather and wool · two workshops
2.text: Two small workshops sew the other half of the Australian scene by hand, and the work has ended up in the best pro shops in the country — Big Dog’s covers sit at Royal Melbourne, Barnbougle and Cape Wickham. If you are going, start here rather than at the logoed cap.
2.old: The other half of the Australian scene is two small workshops sewing things by hand, and their work has quietly ended up in the best pro shops in the country. Big Dog’s covers are in the shops at Royal Melbourne, Barnbougle, Royal Adelaide and Cape Wickham. If you are going and want to bring something home, start here rather than with a logoed cap.

3.label: Two featured · ten more compared
3.text: Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip; no other golf-media or apparel brand in the world does. Across roughly twenty operators, not one described a private Sandbelt tee time as guaranteed — access is sold as capability, never as contract.
3.old: Here is the finding that shaped this section. Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip. No other golf-media or apparel brand in the world does — not No Laying Up, not Fried Egg, not The Golfer’s Journal, none of the clothing labels. Fried Egg has the deposit-and-calendar machinery built and points its whole international programme at Britain and Ireland. Two trips get the full treatment below because they are the two genuinely distinctive things you can book; the other ten are compared underneath on the numbers that actually differ. One thing to carry through all of it: across roughly twenty operators, not one described a private Sandbelt tee time as guaranteed. Access is sold as capability, never as contract.

4.label: The other ten
4.text: The other ten are best compared on price and round count rather than on marketing. Read the AUSGOLF line carefully: that A$2,525 is a rate for Golf Australia members, and overseas surcharges apply without being quantified. Premier’s low headline buys four rounds across ten days.
4.old: Competent, mostly quote-only, and best compared on price and round count rather than on marketing. Read the AUSGOLF line carefully — that A$2,525 is a rate for Golf Australia members, and overseas surcharges apply without being quantified. Premier’s low headline buys four rounds across ten days, not the seven you get elsewhere.

1.html: Australia is the best golf destination almost no American has been to, and the problem is information rather than distance. Half of what gets written about the Melbourne Sandbelt in the US repeats a myth about Alister MacKenzie designing all of it, and almost none of it tells you what a trip costs or how you get on one.
1.old: Australia is the best golf destination almost no American has been to, and the reason is not distance. It is that the information is bad. Half of what gets written about the Melbourne Sandbelt in the US repeats a myth about Alister MacKenzie designing all of it; almost none of it tells you what a trip costs or how you get on one.

2.html: Two things are going on down there. The independent apparel and leather brands have got very good very fast, and nobody outside Australia is covering them properly. Alongside them sits a small set of organised trips an American can book, with prices exactly as published and a clear note where an operator publishes none.
2.old: So this is two lists. The first is the independent brands, which have got very good very fast and which nobody outside Australia is covering properly. The second is every organised trip we could find that an American can actually book, with prices exactly as published and a clear note where they are not.

3.html: Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip, and no other golf media or apparel brand in the world does. The rest of the field sits it out: No Laying Up, Fried Egg, The Golfer’s Journal, Bob Does Sports, Good Good, Skratch, and a dozen clothing labels from Manors to Malbon to Eastside. Fried Egg has a deposit system and a calendar published a year ahead, and points its entire international programme at Britain and Ireland. That leaves a hole in the market, and for now one fourteen-person van tour is filling it.
3.old: The finding that surprised us most is in the second list. Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip. No other golf media or apparel brand does. We checked No Laying Up, Fried Egg, The Golfer’s Journal, Bob Does Sports, Good Good, Skratch, and a dozen clothing labels from Manors to Malbon to Eastside. Nothing. Fried Egg has a deposit system and a calendar published a year ahead, and points its entire international programme at Britain and Ireland. There is a genuine hole in this market, and for now one fourteen-person van tour is filling it.

4.html: Brand prices are in Australian dollars, because that is what these businesses charge. At late-August 2026 rates an Australian dollar is about seventy-two US cents, so knock off a bit under a third. Trip prices are quoted in whatever currency the operator publishes, and each one is labelled. Where an operator publishes no price at all, that is noted rather than guessed at.
4.old: One note on money running through everything below. Brand prices are in Australian dollars, because that is what these businesses charge; at late-August 2026 rates an Australian dollar is about seventy-two US cents, so knock off a bit under a third. Trip prices are quoted in whatever currency the operator publishes, and we have said which. Where an operator does not publish a price, we have said that too, rather than guessing.

#1.name: Original Jones Bag - Evergreen · $215
#1.desc: Evergreen is the Heritage Original, built in what Jones call deluxe vegan leather, and at $215 it is the most expensive version of the bag. The material is the only thing separating it from the $125 Burnt Clay, since the 2.9-lb body and three-way divider underneath are identical.
#1.old: The Heritage version in what Jones calls deluxe vegan leather. The most expensive Original at $215.

#2.name: Original Jones Bag - Espresso · $185
#2.desc: Espresso comes from Painted Hills, a group Jones say is inspired by the landscape of Eastern Oregon, and it is built in industrial canvas. Canvas takes marks in a way ripstop does not, so the bag will look older than it is inside a season, which at $185 is rather the point.
#2.old: Painted Hills, which Jones say is inspired by the landscape of Eastern Oregon. Industrial canvas.

#3.name: Original Jones Bag - Burnt Clay · $125
#3.desc: Burnt Clay is the cheapest way into an Original at $125, and it is the same bag underneath as the $215 one. Jones price the line on material rather than construction, which is why the entry point still carries the three-way divider and the unstructured spine that made the shape.
#3.old: The cheapest way into an Original at $125, and the same bag underneath.

#4.name: Original Jones Bag - Navy/Red/White · $175
#4.desc: Navy, red and white is the core Jones colourway, here in water-resistant nylon at $175. It is the one that looks like the old photographs, which for a shape the company has been making since 1971 is most of the reason to buy an Original in the first place.
#4.old: Water-resistant nylon in the core colourway. This is the one that looks like the old photographs.

#5.name: Original Jones Bag - Moss · $185
#5.desc: Moss is the third Painted Hills colour and the second canvas Original in the line, at $185. Canvas will mark and soften with use, so this is the version that ends up looking like it has been somewhere rather than like it came out of a box.
#5.old: The third Painted Hills colour. Canvas, so it will mark and soften.

#6.name: Utility X - Pageant Blue · $345
#6.desc: The Utility X is the flagship stand bag — 5.1 lbs, a four-way divider and an insulated cooler pocket built into the body. That pocket is the part that separates it from every other stand bag Jones make. Pageant Blue is the brighter of its two colourways, at $345.
#6.old: The flagship. 5.1 lbs, four-way divider, and an insulated cooler pocket built into the bag.

#7.name: Utility X - Graystone · $345
#7.desc: Graystone is a 300d recycled ripstop with a wax-effect coating, and Jones say it develops “a character that is earned, not manufactured.” The claim is doing some work, though the coating does mark and darken with handling. Underneath it is the same $345 Utility X, cooler pocket and all.
#7.old: Graystone is a 300d recycled ripstop with a wax-effect coating. Jones say it develops “a character that is earned, not manufactured.”

#8.name: Trouper - Evergreen/Kodiak · $375
#8.desc: The Trouper is the five-way-divider bag in the range, and this is the Heritage version in vegan leather with Kodiak trim at $375. Five ways is more organisation than most walkers need and about right for anyone carrying a full set plus a jacket. It is the most expensive stand bag Jones make.
#8.old: The Heritage Trouper in vegan leather, five-way divider, $375.

#9.name: Trouper - Olive Gray · $315
#9.desc: Olive Gray is the standard Trouper at $315, the same five-way bag in F-35 recycled ripstop rather than vegan leather. Sixty dollars separates it from the Heritage version and all of that sits in the material, which is how Jones price every line they run.
#9.old: The standard Trouper at $315, which is the same bag in ripstop rather than vegan leather.

#10.name: Rover Stand Bag - High Desert · $295
#10.desc: Jones bill the Rover as their lightest stand bag — 4.2 lbs with a three-way divider — which puts it a pound under the Utility X. High Desert is the warmer of its two colourways at $295. The Rover is the stand bag for people who would otherwise be carrying an Original.
#10.old: Jones bill the Rover as their lightest stand bag — 4.2 lbs, three-way divider.

#11.name: Rover Stand Bag - Graystone · $295
#11.desc: The Rover in Graystone puts the wax-effect ripstop on the lightest stand bag Jones build, at $295. It is the best-looking thing they make, and the coating is the reason. Grey with a waxed face reads like waxed cotton without carrying any of the weight.
#11.old: The Rover in the wax-effect Graystone fabric, which is the best-looking thing they make.

#12.name: Short Course Bag - Navy · $195
#12.desc: The Short Course is built for ten clubs and an afternoon, four pounds with a cooler pocket, in navy at $195. Ten clubs is the right number for a nine-hole loop, and the bag is cut small enough that you notice the difference on your shoulder.
#12.old: Built for ten clubs and an afternoon, with a cooler pocket. Four pounds.

#13.name: Jr. Trouper - Dark Green · $185
#13.desc: Jones scaled the Trouper for ages eight to twelve and kept the four-way divider, in dark green at $185. They did not build a toy version of it. The construction matches the adult bag, and the only thing that changed is the length of the frame the kid carries.
#13.old: A real Trouper scaled for ages eight to twelve, four-way divider. Not a toy.

#14.name: Players Series - Ecru · $225 · sold out
#14.desc: Ecru is the Heritage end of the Players Series at $225, with the structured spine and two-way divider that separate the line from the Original. Ecru on a golf bag shows everything it touches, which is the trade you make for how it looks the day it arrives.
#14.old: Structured spine, two-way divider. The Heritage Ecru is the $225 end of the Players Series.

#15.name: Players Series - Deep Green/Kodiak · $195
#15.desc: Deep Green is the same Players Series bag at $195, trimmed in Kodiak, the vegan leather Jones use across the Heritage line. Thirty dollars under the Ecru and considerably easier to keep clean. The structured spine is the point, since it stands up where an Original slumps.
#15.old: The same bag at $195. Kodiak is the vegan leather trim Jones use across the Heritage line.

#16.name: Rider Bag - Sienna · $520 · sold out
#16.desc: The Rider is the only cart bag Jones make and the most expensive thing in the range at $520. Sienna is the warmer of the two colourways. A cart bag sits upright in front of you for four hours and gets looked at the whole time, which is a fair argument for the better colour.
#16.old: The only cart bag Jones make, and the most expensive item in the range at $520.

#17.name: Rider Bag - Navy/Red/White · $520
#17.desc: The Rider also comes in the house navy, red and white, at the same $520. It is the same cart bag in the colours the brand has run since the beginning, which for a lot of people is the only version of a Jones bag that counts.
#17.old: The Rider in the house colourway.

#18.name: Jones Sports Co. RS by Payntr Golf - White/Field Khaki · $200 · sold out
#18.desc: Jones announced the RS in May 2026 and it is the first shoe the company has put its name on, in white with field khaki at $200. Matt Lemman’s line on it: a shoe that “looks and feels like Jones, but performs at the highest level the game demands.”
#18.old: Announced May 2026 and the first Jones shoe. Matt Lemman’s line on it: a shoe that “looks and feels like Jones, but performs at the highest level the game demands.”

#19.name: Jones Sports Co. RS by Payntr Golf - Gray/Olive · $200 · sold out
#19.desc: Gray and olive is the second colourway, and the division of labour is clean: PAYNTR do the sole, Jones do the rest. That is the sensible way for a bag company to enter footwear. Olive is also the version that sits with the rest of the range at $200.
#19.old: The second colourway. PAYNTR do the sole, Jones do the rest.

#20.name: Beams Passenger Tote - Bronze · $70
#20.desc: The Passenger Tote is one of five pieces Jones made for BEAMS, in a bronze canvas woven for the Japanese retailer’s fiftieth. At $70 it carries that fabric across the biggest surface in the capsule, which is the reason to take it over the dopp kit.
#20.old: Part of a five-piece capsule for the Japanese retailer’s fiftieth, in a bronze canvas made for it.

#21.name: Beams Dopp Kit - Bronze · $45
#21.desc: The dopp kit uses the same bronze canvas from the same BEAMS capsule, at $45. It is the cheapest thing in the collaboration and the piece most likely to leave the golf course, since a dopp kit does the same job wherever you take it.

#22.name: Clockwork Hoodie - Steel Blue · $125
#22.desc: Jones made the Clockwork Hoodie with Standard Issue, in steel blue at $125. It is the only apparel collaboration they have running, which is notable for a company that otherwise puts its name on hard goods. Steel blue keeps it closer to the bag range than to a logo hoodie.
#22.old: With Standard Issue. The only apparel collaboration currently live.

#23.name: Jones X Lusso Cloud Scenario Slide - Rocket Swirl · $80 · sold out
#23.desc: Lusso Cloud make the slide and Jones co-designed it, which is how a recovery shoe ends up in a colourway called Rocket Swirl. At $80 it is the after-round object in the range and the least serious thing the brand has put its name on. It is also the only other piece of footwear they do.
#23.old: Co-designed with Lusso Cloud, who make the slide. A recovery shoe with a Jones sensibility.

#24.name: Michigan St. Rover Stand - Dark Green · $365
#24.desc: The Rover in Michigan State dark green is $365, against $295 for the same bag in the standard line. Seventy dollars is what the official licence costs, and the bag underneath is the same 4.2-lb three-way Rover. Buy it for the school or do not buy it.
#24.old: The Rover in Michigan State colours. $365 against $295 for the same bag in the standard line.

#25.name: Georgia Original Jones Stripeshow - White · $210
#25.desc: The Stripeshow is the Original with a stripe run through it, here in Georgia colours and in what Jones call leather-look vinyl, at $210. Vinyl wipes clean, which matters more on a white bag than on anything else in the Campus line. The licence accounts for the price against a $175 nylon Original.
#25.old: The Stripeshow Original in Georgia colours, in what Jones call leather-look vinyl.

#26.name: Missouri Trouper - Onyx/Kodiak · $410
#26.desc: At $410 the Missouri Trouper is the most expensive bag in the Campus line, because it stacks Heritage trim on top of the licence. Onyx with Kodiak is the same combination Jones charge $375 for without a school on it, and the bag is otherwise unchanged.
#26.old: The most expensive Campus bag at $410 — Heritage trim plus the licence.

#27.name: Circa '71 Headcover w/ Sock - Black · $60
#27.desc: The Circa ’71 covers are named for the founding year and are the only headcovers Jones make. This is the black one with a sock at $60, which is the version that protects a shaft as well as a head. It is the plainest thing in the accessories line.
#27.old: Named for the founding year, with a sock. The only headcovers Jones make.

#28.name: Circa '71 Headcover - Orange · $55
#28.desc: Orange is the sockless Circa ’71 at $55, five dollars under the version with a sock. Sockless suits a driver that lives in a bag with a full divider, where the shaft is already separated from everything else. Orange also makes the cover findable in a way black does not.

#29.name: A2 Backpack - Graystone · $160
#29.desc: The A2 puts the Graystone treatment on a backpack, which Jones list as F-35 recycled ripstop with a soft-hand PU face, at $160. It is the same fabric as the Rover, so the pack and the bag will age at the same rate if you carry both.
#29.old: The A2 in the wax-effect Graystone, which Jones list as F-35 recycled ripstop with a soft-hand PU face.

#30.name: Out of Office Backpack - Wheat/Black · $65
#30.desc: The Out of Office is the cheapest pack Jones sell at $65 and the least golf-looking thing they make. Wheat with black trim reads as a commuter bag rather than a range bag, which is the point of the name and most of the reason to own it.
#30.old: The cheapest pack they sell at $65, and the least golf-looking thing in the range.

#31.name: Range Hoodie - Pageant Blue · $148
#31.desc: The Range Hoodie comes from Forrester’s, the outerwear label Jones own and revived, and their own copy calls it “The original golf outerwear since 1951.” Pageant Blue at $148 puts a 1951 label in the same colour Jones run on the Utility X, which ties the two ends of the range together.
#31.old: Forrester’s, the outerwear label Jones own and revived. Their own copy: “The original golf outerwear since 1951.”

#32.name: Arizona Rangefinder Pouch - Alpine · $77
#32.desc: Jones make forty-odd rangefinder pouches, which is a strange number for an accessory, and this is the Heritage-trimmed one in Arizona colours at $77. Heritage trim means Kodiak vegan leather on the edges. Seventy-seven dollars for a pouch is what a school licence does to a small object.
#32.old: Jones make forty-odd rangefinder pouches. This is the Heritage-trimmed one in Arizona colours.

1.label: The 1971 Bag, Still Made

1.html: Jones makes the best carry bag in golf by leaving things off it — no legs, no cart strap, no panelling to break the surface — and has been doing that from Portland, Oregon since 1971. The founding story is better than most because it is small. George Jones was a forty-year-old taxi driver who sewed the first bags in his basement and sold them out of the trunk of his cab. Jones still tells it that way on their own history page, and finishes the thought with a line that is hard to improve on: “Who could have known? George Jones, that’s who.”

2.html: What their site skips is the middle. George sold the company in 1990, and the new owners tried to make a Jones bag compete with the big manufacturers by making it less like a Jones bag. By the early 2000s the brand was effectively gone. The Lemman family and Chris Carnahan bought it in 2011, and what they bought was almost nothing: no patterns, no inventory, no factory. Matt Lemman, asked later what came with the deal: “Just the name, that was all.”

1.html: Criquet makes golf shirts that never announce themselves as golf shirts, which is how the same four-button placket ends up on a Butler tee box and at a South Congress bar three hours later. Billy Nachman and Hobson Brown have known each other since kindergarten in Manhattan, where they grew up in prep-school polos and coat-and-tie dress codes, and they started the company in Austin in 2010. It begins in a closet, with the vintage golf shirt Nachman’s grandfather left behind: four buttons, a long placket, a collar that had opinions. They rebuilt it with a flap chest pocket, removable collar stays so the collar never bacons at the tip, and an organic-cotton pitch that was ahead of its time, and called it the Players Shirt. It runs in 100 per cent Peruvian pima today and still costs ninety-eight dollars.

The short version: two friends who met in kindergarten in Manhattan — Billy Nachman and Hobson Brown, raised in prep-school polos and coat-and-tie dress codes — moved the idea to Austin and founded Criquet in 2010. The longer version starts in a closet, with the vintage golf shirt Nachman’s grandfather left behind: four buttons, a long placket, a collar that had opinions. They rebuilt it — flap pocket, removable collar stays, an organic-cotton pitch that was ahead of its schedule — and called it the Players Shirt.

2.html: The name comes from the sound of crickets, by the brand’s own telling: the noise of being comfortably off-course. Criquet has never fully committed to being a golf brand. One half of the catalogue is Range Polos in brrr°, a mineral-infused yarn that moves heat off the skin, and Players Shirts you could tee off in at Butler. The other half runs pearl snaps, fine-wale corduroy in burnt orange and a loop-terry shirt called Midnight Toker, which belongs on a pool deck more than a first tee. The two halves hang in the same closet.

3.html: Criquet is an Austin company in a way that shows up in the product. The longtime clubhouse-headquarters on South First had a putting green, an outdoor bar and a Bill Murray mural. Discmania, the Finnish house that supplies most of disc golf, printed the brand’s mascot Carl onto a three-disc set. 1.html: Left of Field is the funniest brand in golf that also makes clothes you would wear without the joke attached. Nick Ilias has run it out of Sydney for four years, starting in 2022 in his brother’s old bedroom, which he described in a journal entry written in Paris three years later as “a small room filled with everything from late-night brainstorming sessions to boxes stacked high with stock.”
1.old: Left of Field Golf is four years old and runs out of Sydney. Nick Ilias started it in 2022 in his brother’s old bedroom — his words, from a journal entry he wrote in Paris three years later: “a small room filled with everything from late-night brainstorming sessions to boxes stacked high with stock.”

2.html: Ilias started from a complaint a lot of players will recognise. “When I first started playing the game, getting dressed for golf felt like a lose-lose situation. The outfits I wanted to wear made me feel out of place in the pro shop. Adhering to the dress code just didn’t feel natural, either.”
2.old: The founding complaint is one a lot of people will recognise. “When I first started playing the game, getting dressed for golf felt like a lose-lose situation. The outfits I wanted to wear made me feel out of place in the pro shop. Adhering to the dress code just didn’t feel natural, either.”

3.html: What he built is not, as it is often described, a brand about Australian landscapes. It is a brand about silhouette. The aim in their own words is clothing “inspired by the attitude and silhouettes of surf and skate apparel, with design touches golfers can appreciate as their own,” and then, flatly: “Our mission isn’t to create products that scream ‘golf’.” That is why the shorts are roomy and cut to sit just above the knee, and why the trousers are pleated and wide. The tees follow the same logic, mid-weight and closer to a skate shirt than a golf one.
3.old: What he built instead is not, as it is often described, a brand about Australian landscapes. It is a brand about silhouette. In their own words the aim is clothing “inspired by the attitude and silhouettes of surf and skate apparel, with design touches golfers can appreciate as their own,” and then, flatly: “Our mission isn’t to create products that scream ‘golf’.” That is why the shorts are roomy and the trousers are pleated and wide, and it is the single most useful thing to know before you look at any of it.

4.html: The landscape part is real, but it operates one level down, in the naming. Every collection ties to a specific stretch of Australian coast and the products take their names from places inside it. Elements is Barnbougle in Tasmania, photographed on the same ground. SOUTH is the Mornington Peninsula. RNP is Royal National Park, south of Sydney. The earliest polos were named after beaches in Sydney Harbour, the one case where they said so outright: “the Clontarf and Nielsen, named after iconic beaches within Sydney Harbour.”
4.old: The landscape part is real, but it operates one level down, in the naming. Every collection is tied to a specific stretch of Australian coast and the products take their names from places inside it. Elements is Barnbougle in Tasmania. SOUTH is the Mornington Peninsula. RNP is Royal National Park, south of Sydney. The earliest polos were named after beaches in Sydney Harbour, which is the one case where they said so outright: “the Clontarf and Nielsen, named after iconic beaches within Sydney Harbour.”

5.html: Two other things stand out. They spent seven months sampling fabric before releasing their first polo, landed on a recycled-PET yarn, and wrote about it plainly: “We know we are stepping into an industry which is regarded as one of the biggest polluters on earth. But we don’t plan to follow the footsteps of the past.” In February 2025 they showed at the Paris Golf Gallery during fashion week, their first international outing, in a room shared with Hiroki, Club 72 and Parmore.

That is Midiron approving itself — Golf Apparel Research is their own house descriptor, carried with a ™ in their Instagram name and embroidered onto the goods. Then each page adds its own warning. The Field Camo: hard to spot, impossible to forget. The Tree Camo: may attract unsolicited ‘where’d you get that?’ questions. The black one: you’ll stop wearing your other caps. Three of the six below are gone.

brown-mock-neck.name: Brown Mock Neck
brown-mock-neck.desc: The mock neck is Rouqe’s signature silhouette and the brown is the clearest version of it — short sleeves, deep chocolate, shot in the brand’s own campaign against dry grass and a cart path at golden hour. They cut it in six colours. In a category where nearly everyone defaults to a three-button placket, the mock is the whole differentiator.
brown-mock-neck.old: The piece that sums the brand up. A short-sleeve mock in a deep chocolate brown, worn in their own campaign against dry grass and a cart path at golden hour. The mock neck is Rouqe’s signature silhouette — they make it in six colours and it is the thing that separates them from every label defaulting to a three-button placket.

burgundy-stripe.name: Burgundy Striped Polo
burgundy-stripe.desc: Wide burgundy and cream rugby stripes run across a boxy body, styled in the campaign with a navy script cap. It reads 1974 club pro rather than 2026 performance polo, which is the register Rouqe handles best. The stripe sold out before anything else in the men’s range.
burgundy-stripe.old: The best-looking thing they have made. Wide burgundy and cream rugby stripes, boxy through the body, worn in the campaign with a navy script cap. It reads more 1974 club pro than 2026 performance polo, and it is gone — which tells you what the customer responded to.

blue-blade-collar.name: Blue Blade Collar
blue-blade-collar.desc: Rouqe cuts this in pale blue with a blade collar and no placket buttons visible from the front, which makes it the cleanest men’s piece in the range. The brand shoots it against a bleached hillside and lets the colour carry the frame. It photographs better on course than anything else they make.
blue-blade-collar.old: Pale blue, blade collar, no placket buttons visible from the front. The cleanest men’s piece in the range and the one that photographs best on course — their own shoot puts it against a bleached hillside and lets the colour do the work.

green-mock-neck.name: Green Mock Neck
green-mock-neck.desc: Sage green is the colour Rouqe keeps returning to across both collections, and here it lands on the same mock silhouette as the brown. The shoot puts it on a hilltop tee with a valley and a lake behind it, which is a long way from the white-cyc studio most labels this size can afford.
green-mock-neck.old: Sage green, the colour the brand keeps returning to across both collections. Same mock silhouette as the brown. Shot on a hilltop tee with a valley and a lake behind, which is a long way from the usual white-cyc studio most labels this size can afford.

script-ls.name: Script Long-Sleeve Polo
script-ls.desc: Black with cream banding across the chest and a cursive script logo, this is the most overtly retro thing Rouqe makes and the most expensive men’s piece at seventy-nine dollars. The long sleeve gives the banding more room to run than the short-sleeve versions allow.
script-ls.old: Black with cream banding across the chest and a cursive script logo. The most overtly retro thing they make, and the most expensive men’s piece at seventy-nine dollars. Also sold out, which is the recurring theme here.

bw-stripe.name: B/W Striped Polo
bw-stripe.desc: Fine black and cream horizontal stripes sit under a white collar and placket, closer to a Breton than to a golf shirt. The scale of the stripe is what does it, narrow enough to read as a knit rather than as sportswear. You could wear it to lunch afterward without anyone asking about your round.
bw-stripe.old: Fine black and cream horizontal stripes with a white collar and placket. Closer to a Breton than a golf shirt. Where the burgundy is loud, this is the version you could wear to lunch afterwards without anyone asking about your round.

two-tone.name: Two Tone Polo Blue
two-tone.desc: A royal blue yoke sits over a white body with the script mark kept small at the back of the neck. Colour-blocked shapes like this have moved in and out of golf since the eighties, almost always with contrast piping along the seam. Rouqe leaves the piping off and the shape is cleaner for it.
two-tone.old: Royal blue yoke over a white body, with the script mark small on the back of the neck. A colour-blocked shape that has been in and out of golf since the eighties, executed here without the usual contrast piping.

eagle-polo.name: Eagle Polo Black
eagle-polo.desc: Plain black with a small embroidered eagle at the chest, and the studio photography goes dark to match — hard light, black background, styled far closer to a streetwear campaign than a golf catalogue. The simplicity of the garment is what lets the lighting do that much work.
eagle-polo.old: Plain black with a small embroidered eagle at the chest. Their studio photography goes dark and moody for this one — hard light, black background, styled far closer to a streetwear campaign than a golf catalogue.

roq-polo.name: ROQ Polo
roq-polo.desc: An all-over black and white print sits somewhere near houndstooth, finished with a solid white collar. It is the busiest thing in the men’s range and a useful reminder that Rouqe does not only make quiet tonal basics. The white collar keeps the print from taking the whole shirt over.
roq-polo.old: An all-over black and white houndstooth-adjacent print with a solid white collar. The busiest thing in the men’s range and a reminder that Rouqe is not only doing quiet tonal basics.

knit-beige.name: “R” Knit Sweater Beige
knit-beige.desc: A cream knit carries an outsized cursive R across the front in a contrasting tone, and it works better in the clubhouse than in the swing. Rouqe prices it thirty dollars under the black version of the same sweater. The knit has enough body to hold the letterform without puckering around it.
knit-beige.old: Cream knit with an outsized cursive R across the front in a contrasting tone. The kind of piece that works better in the clubhouse than in the swing, and priced thirty dollars under the black version of the same sweater.

rq-sweater.name: RQ Sweater
rq-sweater.desc: A cream chevron cuts across the chest of a black crewneck and that is the entire design — Rouqe’s whole argument in one garment. They shoot it against deep maroon with a putter in frame and a squint that says the club championship is already decided. Rouqe prices its knitwear like it wants you to actually buy it.
rq-sweater.old: The value item of the whole store. Black with a cream chevron across the chest, thirty-nine dollars, and shot in the campaign against a deep maroon studio backdrop with a putter and a cigarette-club-champion energy that the price does not suggest.

w-dress-black.name: “R” Dress Black
w-dress-black.desc: The R Dress is the flagship and the most expensive piece Rouqe makes: sleeveless, collared, cut close through the body with a pleated skirt that moves. The brand shoots it on a fairway with mountains behind and no styling tricks at all. Both colourways have sold out.

w-dress-pink.name: “R” Dress Pink

range-tee.name: Range Tee Black

So has the black long-sleeve with the cream chest banding, and so has the houndstooth. Twelve of the twenty-one pieces in the men’s collection are gone, and the loudest ones went first, which tells you more about the brand than a fabric spec would.

2.html: What is left is a small and unusually coherent range. The mock neck is the silhouette everything is built on, cut in six colours at fifty-nine dollars, in a category where nearly everyone defaults to a three-button placket. Around it sit retro stripes and a palette of sage green, chocolate brown, burgundy and cream that runs across both lines. The brown mock neck and the brown skort are shot on the same couple, which is more coordination than most labels this size bother with.

3.html: The photography is the other thing. Rouqe shoots two ways: hard-lit studio portraits against black and deep maroon, styled closer to a streetwear campaign than a golf catalogue, and on-course work at golden hour on a dry mountain course with a lake in the middle distance. Every image on the site is the brand’s own, and it carries more atmosphere than labels ten times the size manage.

4.html: What Rouqe will not tell you is who runs it. There is no About page, and the URL returns a 404. No founder is named on the store or in any interview, and the domain registration is privacy-shielded. The one person publicly attached to the brand is Marko Mijaljevic, its Head of Design, credited with the SS25 collection. The domain was registered in spring 2023, which dates the shopfront rather than the company. For a label whose whole pitch is a point of view, the anonymity is a strange choice, and the clothes are good enough that it is the only thing holding the story back.

patriot-driver.desc: The Patriot is the civilian version of the most famous thing Seamus has made. Matt Kuchar commissioned American flag covers for the entire 2016 U.S. Ryder Cup team, each one carrying thirteen hand-cut stripes and fifty embroidered stars, and the standing line runs on that same DNA. It is wool, cut and sewn in Beaverton and fleece-lined like everything the shop makes.

glacier-driver.name: Pendleton® Glacier Peaks Wool Driver · $150
glacier-driver.desc: Megan Chisti was a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills when she sewed the first Seamus cover, and the licensed Pendleton line closes that loop. Glacier Peaks is the Pacific Northwest blanket pattern, and in wool on a driver it is the cover Seamus customers buy more than any other.

dude-driver.name: “The Dude” Natural Canvas Driver · $155

sugarskulls-mallet.name: Pendleton® Sugar Skulls Heel Shafted Mallet · $150

sugarskulls-mallet.old: The loudest thing in the Pendleton license and a house best seller in five different cover shapes — a Día de los Muertos skull motif in full color. The mallet is the shape that shows the most of the print.

harristweed-putter.name: Navy Harris Tweed Blade Putter · $130
harristweed-putter.desc: Harris Tweed is the only fabric in the world protected by its own act of parliament, hand-woven in the Outer Hebrides and certified with an orb stamp. Seamus imports it and cuts it into blade covers in Oregon. The navy herringbone will outlast several putters.
harristweed-putter.old: Harris Tweed is the world’s only fabric protected by its own act of parliament — hand-woven in the Outer Hebrides, certified by orb stamp. Seamus imports it and cuts it into blade covers in Oregon. A navy herringbone that will outlast several putters.

limerick-marker.name: Hand Forged® Limerick Ball Marker — Bronze · $48
limerick-marker.desc: The Limerick is the top seller in the Hand Forged program, and every one is hammered rather than cast or poured. Seamus’s blacksmith works in Portland and now does roughly ninety per cent of his business with the brand. Personalization is hand-stamped up to five characters and costs nothing.
limerick-marker.old: The top-selling piece of the Hand Forged program. Every one is hammered — not cast, not poured — by Seamus’s blacksmith in Portland, who now does roughly ninety per cent of his business with the brand, and hand-stamped personalization up to five characters is free.

drainit-marker.name: Hand Forged® “Drain It” Ball Marker — Steel · $48
drainit-marker.desc: The marker says exactly what you are supposed to do next, and it is hammered into steel by hand in the Portland smithy. Every forged piece comes out a little different from the last, which is the point of the Hand Forged line. Yours will not match anyone else’s.
drainit-marker.old: A hammered steel marker that says exactly what you are supposed to do next. The forged pieces come out of the smithy slightly different every time, which is the point — yours will not match anyone else’s.

sugarskulls-marker.name: Hand Forged® Pendleton® Sugar Skulls Marker — Oil Can · $36
sugarskulls-marker.desc: Licensed Pendleton patterns and blacksmith-made markers are the two things Seamus does that nobody else does, and this is the point where they cross. The Sugar Skulls print is translated into hammered metal and finished oil-can dark, the Día de los Muertos motif carried in texture rather than in the full color it gets on wool.
sugarskulls-marker.old: The Sugar Skulls print translated into hammered metal with an oil-can finish — the crossover point of the two things Seamus does that nobody else does: licensed Pendleton patterns and blacksmith-made markers.

horseshoe-marker.name: Hand Forged® Lucky Horseshoe Marker — Steel · $48
horseshoe-marker.desc: Seamus keeps a whole category of superstition markers, which is not something any other brand has thought to do, and the horseshoe is the best seller in it. It is hand-hammered steel, sized to carry to the first tee instead of hanging over a door.
horseshoe-marker.old: A horseshoe you can actually carry to the first tee. Steel, hand-hammered, and the best-selling of the superstition markers — a category only Seamus would think to have.

markit8-marker.name: Hand Forged® “Mark It 8” Marker — Copper · $36
markit8-marker.desc: The Mark It 8 marker completes the Lebowski set that the Dude cover and mallet begin, this one hammered in copper rather than steel. It is made for anyone who has ever wanted to mark it eight on a scorecard where an eight would be the generous number, which at $36 is a cheap enough joke to carry in a pocket.
markit8-marker.old: The Lebowski reference completing the set with the Dude covers above — a copper marker for anyone who has ever wanted to mark it eight on a card where that would be generous. Over the line? No. $36.

goat-tag.name: Hand Forged® Goat Caddie Bottle-Opener Bag Tag · $76
goat-tag.desc: The bag tag is hammered steel in the shape of the Seamus goat-caddie mark, and it doubles as a bottle opener. It comes out of the same Portland smithy as the markers, one piece at a time. It hangs on the bag looking decorative until roughly the ninth hole, at which point $76 starts to look well spent.
goat-tag.old: A steel bag tag that is also a bottle opener, hammered into the shape of the brand’s goat-caddie mark. The most useful $76 on this page by roughly the ninth hole.

canyonlands-towel.name: Canyonlands Golf Towel · $45
canyonlands-towel.desc: Canyonlands is the Pendleton desert geometric woven as a jacquard towel, which puts the pattern into the cloth rather than printing it on top. The towel line keeps landing on the Seamus best-seller list. At $45 it is the cheapest way to get one of the blanket patterns onto a bag.
canyonlands-towel.old: The Pendleton desert geometric as a jacquard-woven towel — part of a towel line that keeps landing in their best sellers. At $45 it is the cheapest way to get the blanket patterns onto your bag.

dude-shirt.name: “Obviously You’re Not A Golfer” Dude Shirt · $65
dude-shirt.desc: Seamus makes a shirt, and it is one of their best sellers. The Walter Sobchak line runs across a camp-collar print covered in Dude iconography, which is a lot of joke to hang on one garment. It is still funny on the eighth wear, which is more than most novelty golf shirts manage.
dude-shirt.old: Yes, they make a shirt, and yes, it is a best seller — the Walter Sobchak line on a camp-collar print covered in Dude iconography. The rare piece of golf clothing whose joke actually holds up on the eighth wear.

1.label: Nine covers · $120 to $170
1.text: Driver and fairway covers are the engine of the company, cut and sewn in the Beaverton workshop in wool, leather, canvas and seersucker. Their site also runs a Customizer that builds one-offs out of panels, fasteners and linings.
1.old: Driver and fairway covers are the engine of the company — wool, leather, canvas and seersucker, every one cut and sewn in the Beaverton workshop. There is also a Customizer on their site that lets you mash up panels, fasteners and linings into a one-off; we left it out of the grid only because your version will not look like ours. 2.label: Six covers · $120 to $170
2.text: The putter shelf is where the fabric library shows off: parliament-protected Harris Tweed, registered Irish tartans, Hawaiian barkcloth and licensed Pendleton patterns, fleece-lined and shaped for blades and mallets. It sits closest to the covers Megan Chisti first sewed in the garage.

3.old: The other half of the workshop, straight off the best-seller list: markers hammered by an actual blacksmith in Portland, a bottle-opener bag tag, Pendleton towels and one very quotable shirt. Personalization on the forged pieces is hand-stamped in-house and free.

1.html: Seamus turns the headcover into the most personal object in the bag, in registered Irish tartans and licensed Pendleton wool, and the company started with one that was falling apart. Akbar Chisti’s father had given him a wool cover from a famous links club, Royal Troon by the company’s own telling, and it had worn through. His wife Megan was a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, so in 2011 she remade it from fabric remnants, sewed a few more for his golf group, and then the two of them were running a company out of their garage. It is named after their Irish Terrier, Seamus O’Reily, and you pronounce it SHAY-mus.
1.old: The Seamus origin story runs through a closet, like Criquet’s, except this one starts with a headcover. Akbar Chisti’s father had given him a wool cover from a famous links club — the company’s own telling says Royal Troon — and it was wearing out. His wife Megan happened to be a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, so in 2011 she remade it from fabric remnants, then sewed a few more for his golf group, and then they were running a company out of their garage. It is named after their Irish Terrier, Seamus O’Reily. You pronounce it SHAY-mus.

2.html: The first wholesale order came from Bandon Dunes, where Akbar had caddied in college. Fifteen years later the operation still cuts and sews everything in Beaverton, Oregon, in wool, leather, canvas and seersucker, with fabric from Pendleton and from UK mills including parliament-protected Harris Tweed. It wholesales to roughly 700 shops worldwide and the Chistis still own all of it.
2.old: The first wholesale order came from Bandon Dunes, where Akbar had caddied in college — about as good an origin credential as Pacific Northwest golf can issue. Fifteen years later the operation still cuts and sews everything in Beaverton, Oregon, sources wool from Pendleton and from UK mills including parliament-protected Harris Tweed, and wholesales to roughly 700 shops worldwide while the Chistis still own all of it.

3.html: Two things make Seamus more than a nice accessories company. The first is the 2016 Ryder Cup, when Matt Kuchar commissioned personalized American flag covers for the entire U.S. team: thirteen hand-cut stripes, fifty embroidered stars, each one sewn in Oregon. The second is the blacksmith. The Hand Forged line of markers, pitch tools and money clips is hammered rather than cast, by a smith in Portland who now does about ninety per cent of his business with Seamus. The USGA lets them set up and hammer markers on-site at U.S. Open merchandise pavilions, where the brand has sold every year since Chambers Bay in 2015.

Seamus has appeared in half a dozen of our edits already; this is the page those mentions have been waiting for.

#1.name: Sail Bag “8185” · $975 · Sold out
#1.desc: MacKenzie builds this one from retired sailcloth, so each bag carries the number of the sail it came from — 8185, in this case. Three were made, at $975. It is the piece people bring up when they talk about Sugarloaf, and the reason the waitlist exists at all.
#1.old: Built from retired sailcloth, so each one carries the number of the sail it came from. Three were made. This is the piece people bring up when they talk about SSC, and the reason the waitlist exists.

#2.name: White Leather Double Seve 8” · $1400 · Sold out
#2.desc: White leather on a Double Seve body makes this the most expensive thing Sugarloaf has ever put its name on. MacKenzie builds the same 8-inch bag in canvas for $850, so the hide accounts for the rest of the $1400. White is a bold choice for something you carry across wet grass.
#2.old: The most expensive thing SSC has ever put its name on. White leather on a Double Seve body, which is a bold choice for a bag you carry across wet grass.

#3.name: Double Seve 8” · $850 · Sold out
#3.desc: The standard-issue Double Seve carries the same 8-inch MacKenzie body, in canvas rather than white leather, and it sold at $850. That is the cheaper of the two by a wide margin, though $850 is still $850. Canvas will also scuff and soften in a way the white hide never would.
#3.old: The standard-issue version of the above, in canvas. Still $850, still gone.

#4.name: Shoe Bag · $195
#4.desc: MacKenzie makes the shoe bag in navy canvas with the club crest on the face. It is one of the few pieces from the collaboration you can still buy, and at $195 it is the cheapest way into that work by a factor of four against the bags.
#4.old: Navy canvas with the club crest. One of the few MacKenzie pieces you can still buy, and the cheapest way into that collaboration by a factor of four.

#5.name: “Major” Stripe Sport Polo · $95
#5.desc: A navy, gold and white block stripe runs across the chest in the colours Sugarloaf drew up for TPC Sawgrass. It is an officially licensed PGA Tour product, which usually shows on the garment, and here the stripe carries the design instead of a logo. $95 for the polo.
#5.old: Navy, gold and white block stripe made for TPC Sawgrass. An officially licensed PGA Tour product that doesn't look like one, which is harder than it sounds.

#6.name: Caddie Crew · $110
#6.desc: The Caddie Crew comes in powder blue with the championship mark ringed on the chest. A ring reads collegiate rather than corporate, which is most of the difference between this and standard tournament merchandise. The colour helps too, since navy would have pushed it back towards a uniform.
#6.old: Powder blue crewneck with the championship mark ringed on the chest. Reads collegiate rather than corporate.

#7.name: Tech Vest · $115
#7.desc: The tech vest is black, quarter-zip and close to unbranded, which makes it the most wearable thing in the Sawgrass capsule. A vest with no visible tournament mark does not date the week it was made for. At $115 it goes over a polo in spring and under a shell later.
#7.old: Black, quarter-zip, minimal branding. The most wearable thing in the Sawgrass capsule.

#8.name: Runner Cap · $45
#8.desc: The Runner Cap is a nylon five-panel at $45, still in stock, and the easy way into the tournament work. Five-panel nylon sits flatter on the head than a structured crown, so it packs into a bag and comes back out fine. It is also the cheapest thing in the capsule by half.
#8.old: Nylon five-panel. $45 and still in stock, which makes it the easy entry point to the tournament work.

#9.name: Evans Scholars T-Shirt · $44 · Sold out
#9.desc: Sugarloaf made this one with the Western Golf Association, in washed green with a flag at the chest pocket. The Evans Scholars program sends caddies to college on full housing-and-tuition scholarships, and the line supports it. At $44 it is the cheapest thing the two have done together, and the plainest.
#9.old: Washed green with a chest-pocket flag. The Evans Scholars program sends caddies to college on full housing-and-tuition scholarships, and this line supports it. The best reason on this page to want something restocked.

#10.name: Caddie Sling · $90 · Sold out
#10.desc: A pistachio green pouch hangs off a plain webbing strap, and Sugarloaf shot it on a bag drop rather than a studio table. It is the accessory people ask about, which has more to do with the colour than the format. At $90 it was also one of the cheaper things in the scholarship work.
#10.old: Pistachio green pouch on a webbing strap, shot on a bag drop. Small, cheap, and the one accessory here people ask about.

#11.name: Sport Polo · $95
#11.desc: Sugarloaf made the Sport Polo with the Western Golf Association, and it is the piece from the scholarship run you can still buy at $95. The rest of that line sold through, so a polo is what remains of a collaboration built to put caddies through college on full housing and tuition.
#11.old: Still in stock at $95, which is the exception in this section.

#12.name: “Team Bag” · $375 · Sold out
#12.desc: Sugarloaf built a black carry bag for the Evans Scholars program and priced it at $375, which made it the most expensive piece in that line by a distance. A carry bag is the right object for the cause, given the program exists for people who walk the course with somebody else’s clubs.
#12.old: A black carry bag done for the scholarship program. $375, long gone.

#13.name: Hedgehog Knit Headcover · $105 · Sold out
#13.desc: Clubhaus is a Japanese golf media brand, and the capsule it made with Sugarloaf reads that way from the first piece. The headcover is navy knit with a multicolour tassel and a hedgehog at the crown, which is a more specific animal than most brands would land on. Sugarloaf priced it at $105.
#13.old: Navy knit with a multicolour tassel and a hedgehog at the crown. Clubhaus is a Japanese golf media brand, and the whole capsule reads that way.

#14.name: Sensu Fan · $14
#14.desc: A folding paper sensu fan, printed with the Clubhaus mark, sells for $14 and is the cheapest thing Sugarloaf has ever put its name on. It also explains the brand better than the bags do. The object is paper and one printed mark, and it exists because the collaboration was Japanese.
#14.old: A folding paper sensu fan, printed with the Clubhaus mark, $14. The cheapest thing SSC sells and the one that best explains the brand.

#15.name: Windshirt · $125 · Sold out
#15.desc: The windshirt is black, cropped and quarter-zip, which is about as much as a windshirt needs to be. Cropped is the part that dates it to this collaboration rather than to golf outerwear generally. It went in the first run at $125 and has not come back.
#15.old: Black, cropped, quarter-zip. Sold out in the first run.

#16.name: Valuables Pouch · $135 · Sold out
#16.desc: The valuables pouch is a zip pouch at $135, which is a Japanese-collaboration price if ever there was one. It holds what comes out of your pockets on the first tee and then goes back in the bag. Clubhaus put its mark on it and Sugarloaf sold it out.
#16.old: $135 for a zip pouch, which is a Japanese-collaboration price if ever there was one.

#17.name: “SUMMER P.O.P.” Eighty Seven · $250 · Sold out
#17.desc: PAYNTR builds the Eighty Seven and Sugarloaf did the colourway, which came out white with red detailing through the outsole. It landed in June 2026, timed to the U.S. Open, at $250. Red on a white shoe reads loud in a photograph and much quieter on a course.

#18.name: Summer Slides · $50 · Sold out

#19.name: Rangefinder Case · $95 · Sold out
#19.desc: Sentinel makes everything in Japan and it shows in the hardware, which is the reason to look closely at what is otherwise a rangefinder case. This one is tan cordura with a blue stripe and a purple tab, three colours doing the job a logo does elsewhere, at $95.
#19.old: Tan cordura with a blue stripe and a purple tab. Sentinel makes everything in Japan, and it shows in the hardware.

#20.name: Red Field Jacket · $355 · Sold out
#20.desc: The field jacket is red, sells at $355, and is the most substantial garment Sentinel and Sugarloaf have made together. #26.desc: TOTEM makes the divot tool in brass, in three pieces, at $130. Brass is most of the appeal, because it darkens with handling rather than holding a finish, so the tool ages instead of wearing out. It is the nicest object Sugarloaf sells short of a bag.

#28.desc: The artist Gleezy drew a cartoon quail in golf shoes, and Sugarloaf put it on a $44 t-shirt for a Charlotte-specific run. A city graphic drawn by one artist is the kind of thing a brand does when it has no interest in selling the same shirt everywhere.

#29.desc: The same Charlotte run produced a headcover in purple and teal knit with a lilac tassel, at $95. It is the loudest thing Sugarloaf has made, and knit is the only construction that could carry those colours and the tassel without looking like a mistake.

#32.name: The Tour Towel · $95
#32.desc: The Tour Towel runs a teal stripe and holds at $95, which is a lot for a towel and about standard for this brand. Teal turns up across the stranger corners of the catalogue, and a towel is the easiest place to take it. Still in stock, which most of the archive is not.

#33.name: The Terry Anorak · $165
#33.desc: The anorak is green terry cloth with a quarter-zip, at $165, and it sits in a full terry run that also takes in a cabana shirt, a short and a mini skirt. Terry is a pool fabric before it is a golf fabric, which is most of the reason it works here.

1.html: Sugarloaf Social Club runs the widest price range in independent golf and holds a single point of view across all of it. The catalogue reaches from a MacKenzie sailcloth bag at $1,400 down to a paper fan at $14, and both read as the same company. It started as a group chat. A few college roommates were graduating in 2011 and wanted somewhere to keep talking about golf, so they named the thread after the course they had spent four years on. The chat became an annual trip, and the trip became an Instagram account that at one point had more followers than Golf Digest. Ian Gilley filed the LLC in 2017 and has described the sequence as “a happy little accident.”
1.old: Sugarloaf Social Club was a group chat. The chat became an annual trip. The trip became an Instagram account. At one point that account had more followers than Golf Digest. Ian Gilley filed the LLC in 2017 and has described the whole sequence as “a happy little accident.”

2.html: The course they named it after is dead. Sugarloaf Mountain in Minneola, Florida was Coore & Crenshaw's first design in the state, built in 2008 across more than 250 feet of elevation, and it opened directly into the financial crisis. It never recovered and it is permanently closed. A brand named after a course you can no longer play is an on-the-nose metaphor for how golf nostalgia works, and to their credit SSC has never leaned on it.

3.html: Sugarloaf is a subsidiary of Pro Shop, Inc., the media company founded by Full Swing producer Chad Mumm and Joe Purzycki, which raised around $20 million from the PGA Tour and Powerhouse Capital and also owns Skratch and GolfWRX. Skratch discloses this in its own coverage. It explains how an independent-looking brand from McLean, Virginia ends up with an officially licensed THE PLAYERS capsule in the navy, gold and white it drew up for TPC Sawgrass.

Skratch discloses this in its own coverage. It is why an independent-looking brand from McLean, Virginia has an officially licensed THE PLAYERS capsule.

Most of it has sold out.

#1.name: Legacy Leather Stand Bag · $1,200

1.html: Sun Mountain invented the bag with legs, and four decades on it still makes the lightest way to walk a golf course. In 1981 a club pro named Rick Reimers quit his job in Northern California and got in the car to drive north to Montana, to ski and think. The car radio was broken, so he spent the whole drive designing a golf bag in his head. What came out the other end was a nylon carry bag that weighed less than half what the leather and vinyl bags of the day weighed.
1.old: In 1981 a club pro named Rick Reimers quit his job in Northern California and drove north to Montana to ski and think. The car radio was broken. He spent the whole drive designing a golf bag in his head — and what came out the other end was a nylon carry bag that weighed less than half what the leather and vinyl bags of the day weighed.

2.html: That was the BACK 9, and it was more interesting than it was successful. The FRONT 9 arrived in 1984 with a moulded top and bottom, sold properly, and became the shape every other carry bag copied. It also earned Sun Mountain the job of building the L8 bag for Ping, which put a Missoula startup in the position of manufacturing for one of golf’s giants.
2.old: That was the BACK 9, and it was more interesting than it was successful. The FRONT 9 in 1984 fixed that with a moulded top and bottom, sold properly, and became the shape every other carry bag copied. It also earned Sun Mountain a job building the L8 bag for Ping — a startup in Missoula quietly manufacturing for one of golf’s giants.

3.html: Then, in 1986, they put legs on it. The Eclipse is the bag Sun Mountain is credited with inventing, and its patented stand mechanism is now hinged onto almost every carry bag in the game. They ran the same trick twice more. The Speed Cart in 1999 folded down small enough that people bought one, and a walking-cart category appeared where there had not been one. The ClubGlider in 2008 put retractable legs on a travel bag, so an airport stopped being a workout.
3.old: Then, in 1986, they put legs on it. The Eclipse is the bag Sun Mountain is credited with inventing, the one that patented the stand mechanism now hinged onto essentially every carry bag in the game. They did the same trick twice more: the Speed Cart in 1999 folded small enough that walking carts became something people actually owned, and the ClubGlider in 2008 put retractable legs on a travel bag so an airport stopped being a workout.

4.html: Here is the part that gets left out. Reimers ran the company for 41 years as founder, director and sole shareholder, with no partners, no investors and no board. In March 2022 he sold Sun Mountain Sports to Solace Capital Partners, a Los Angeles private equity firm, and kept the scooter business. The bags are still assembled in Missoula, which remains unusual for the category. The fabrics come from Asia, and the company says “assembled in the USA” rather than made, which is the honest version.

In March 2022 he sold Sun Mountain Sports to Solace Capital Partners, a Los Angeles private equity firm, and kept the scooter business. The bags are still assembled in Missoula, which remains genuinely unusual; the fabrics come from Asia, and the company says “assembled in the USA” rather than made, which is the honest version.

5.html: The line runs across four categories: bags from the $224 Eclipse up to a $1,200 leather stand bag, push carts, travel covers, and small goods down to a $35 headcover. Three of those four are categories Sun Mountain either created or reshaped, which is a strange thing to say about the sensible default.

launderette.name: Launderette
launderette.desc: Launderette took over a 1950s laundromat on Holly Street in 2015 and has been a Michelin Guide listing and a neighborhood room ever since, with a new head chef in the kitchen since December. Order the plancha burger and the wood-grilled octopus, then finish with the birthday cake ice cream sandwich that Eater counts among Austin’s most iconic dishes. The neon sign out front does a lot of the work.
launderette.old: The anchor of this list and the reason it exists. Order the plancha burger, the wood-grilled octopus, and no matter what else happens, the birthday cake ice cream sandwich — Eater has it on the shortlist of Austin’s most iconic dishes. The neon sign alone is date-worthy… scratch that: the neon sign alone closes the argument.

hestia.name: Hestia
hestia.desc: Kevin Fink cooks over live fire at Hestia, and the room held a Michelin star in both 2024 and 2025. The scallops come off the hearth and the sourdough arrives with beef-fat butter, because everything here passes through the flame first. If the weekend included a personal best, this is the room where you tell the story.

uchiko.name: Uchiko
uchiko.desc: Uchiko is Tyson Cole’s flagship sibling and the hardest table of the six, so book weeks out. Ham and eggs — crispy pork belly under a soft yolk — and the jasmine cream brûlée have been settling Austin arguments for fifteen years. Reserve it the same day you reserve the weekend tee times.

sammies.name: Sammie’s Italian

It is the right answer when the second eighteen finished at seven and the evening still needs to feel like an occasion.

este.name: Este
este.desc: Este comes from the Suerte team and cooks coastal Mexican seafood — aguachiles, wood-fired whole fish — out of the prettiest blue building on the east side. The reservation is the hard part. The hour on the patio once you have it is the easiest thing about the whole weekend.

clarks.name: Clark’s Oyster Bar
clarks.desc: Clark’s is a tiny preppy-nautical room on West 6th that has been the city’s default celebration spot since 2012. Order oysters, a lobster roll and something cold and French by the glass. The room is small enough that the reservation is the hard part, though the bar seats reward walk-in optimism.

josephine.name: Josephine House
josephine.desc: Josephine House sits in a blue cottage in Clarksville with a gravel garden patio, next door to its sister restaurant Jeffrey’s. This is the golden-hour option, so go before sunset and take a table outside. The steak frites and the string lights will do the apologizing for a five-hour absence.

oddduck.name: Odd Duck
oddduck.desc: Odd Duck is Bryce Gilmore’s farm-to-table original and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and it started life as a trailer before it turned into an institution. The small plates are the best ordering in town. The move is to hand the menu back and ask the kitchen to feed you.

justines.name: Justine’s Brasserie
justines.desc: Justine’s runs out of a 1937 bungalow in candlelight, seats late and pours later. Steak frites, escargot and a bottle of red arrive with no rush attached to any of it. When the second round ran long and every other kitchen in town is closing, Justine’s is the insurance policy.

canje.name: Canje
canje.desc: Canje is Tavel Bristol-Joseph’s modern Caribbean room, where pepper fish and West Indian curry come out of the kitchen and the rum drinks come off the bar. It is loud, warm and fully alive. Food & Wine ranked it No. 3 on the 2026 Global Tastemakers list.

tfb.name: Texas French Bread

birdies.name: Birdie’s

loro.name: Loro

nixta.name: Nixta Taqueria

matts.name: Matt’s El Rancho

1.html: Here is the math of a 36-hole weekend: ten hours on the course, two more at the range or the bar, and a partner at home who has watched you leave in the dark twice. Dinner stops being a suggestion at that point. Dinner is the peace treaty, and Austin has an unusually good set of rooms to sign it in.

2.html: The rooms run at three volumes. The Splurge is for real occasions and real apologies: the hearth at Hestia, the hardest sushi table at Uchiko, and the 1950s laundromat on Holly Street that Launderette turned into one of Austin’s defining restaurants. And yes, there is a counter-service wine bar in town called Birdie’s, Food & Wine named it Restaurant of the Year in 2023, and it is spectacular.

jan-craig.name: Jan Craig Headcovers · Hand-knit since 1962
jan-craig.desc: Jan was an avid golfer who could not find covers she liked, so she knitted her own on a rural route outside Cincinnati, shared party line and all. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set in the mid-sixties, and Tom Watson and multiple Ryder Cup teams carried them after him. They are still hand-knit to order in 100% worsted wool, $63 to $79, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver covers.

The company is made of Pendleton scrap, and Pendleton became a licensed partner rather than the other way round. The first order was Bandon Dunes. Covers run $110 to $140 in wool, leather, waxed canvas and tweed, and the company registers as women and minority owned.

The first prototypes came off Gail’s inherited sewing machine, which Marc destroyed inside a month. Italian vachetta and Horween leather patina rather than wear out, and the range runs to belts, wallets and scorecard covers.

daphnes.name: Daphne’s Headcovers · Est. 1979
daphnes.desc: Daphne’s invented the animal headcover and made Frank, the tiger Tiger Woods first carried at the 1997 Masters, after which business grew 400% in a quarter.
