1.html: The argument for this group is not who founded the brands but how well the things are made, and Jan Craig is the proof. In 1962 a golfer of that name, out on a rural route outside Cincinnati, made her own headcovers in worsted wool because she could not buy any she liked for a new set of clubs. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years, Tom Watson carried them, and so did multiple Ryder Cup teams. Every cover is still hand-knit to order, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver.

Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years. Tom Watson carried them. So did multiple Ryder Cup teams. The company still hand-knits every cover to order, and the only design change in six decades was adding elastic inside the driver.

2.html: The animal headcover came seventeen years later, from a mother and daughter in Phoenix. Frank, the tiger, went on Tiger Woods’ driver at the 1997 Masters, Nike licensed the character and named him, and the business grew four hundred per cent in a quarter.

3.html: Neither of those is a novelty company, and neither is interesting only for who started it. Seventeen brands do both things at once: founded or co-founded by a woman, and making what men buy, which is headcovers, leather, bags, gloves, towels, socks, polos and shoes. Almost every women-founded golf brand makes women’s apparel and nothing else, and almost every independent brand making unisex hard goods was founded by men, so the overlap between the two runs thin.

That is the post: seventeen brands founded or co-founded by women, filtered to the ones making things men actually buy — headcovers, leather, bags, gloves, towels, socks, polos, shoes. The filter is what made it hard. Almost every women-founded golf brand makes women’s apparel and nothing else, and almost every independent brand making unisex hard goods was founded by men. The overlap is thin enough that finding it meant checking dozens of names one at a time.

4.html: One pattern turns up again and again. Megan Chisti co-founded Seamus, trained as the designer, rebuilt the headcover that started the company and still sews product, and there is no published quote from her anywhere. Gail Hanson co-founded Bluetross, and the first prototypes came off her inherited sewing machine; the biggest feature ever written about the company is headlined “the unlikely story of a man who quit his job to make leather headcovers.” Neither brand is hiding anything, and both credit her plainly on their own About page. The voice just defaults to him. So every entry names the woman, and says plainly when she co-founded with a husband or a mother rather than rounding up.

1.html: The second PUMA Golf and Realtree collection is the one where the camo stops reading as novelty and starts reading as a colourway you would wear off the course. Precision in the Wild is ten pieces, released on Monday, and the interesting part is how differently it behaves from the first one.
1.old: PUMA Golf and Realtree released their second collection together on Monday. It is called Precision in the Wild, it runs to ten pieces, and the interesting part is how differently it behaves from the first one.

2.html: The first drop, in February 2025, was a spectacle. It ran in Realtree Edge, Deep Forest and Rickie Orange, and it arrived on Rickie Fowler head to toe on the Thursday of the WM Phoenix Open, the rowdiest stage in professional golf and chosen deliberately. The second arrived on a Monday in late August in Dusty Olive and Alpine Snow, with no tournament and no player attached to it.

3.html: What it has instead is a new pattern. Realtree Legacy was made for the company’s fortieth anniversary, and it is the first pattern co-designed by founder Bill Jordan and his son Tyler. It takes the dark bark structure of the Original pattern and warms it into browns and warm greys where Original ran cool, with segmented bark lines and drop shadows doing the depth work. On the fleece vest it looks like a hunting layer. On the spikeless HELSINKI G runner it reads as a shoe you would keep on off the course.

4.html: PUMA has form here. The Volition America line has carried camo golf shirts for years in patriotic red, white and blue for Folds of Honor. Realtree gives PUMA the same visual language with outdoor-industry provenance behind it, which is the argument PUMA itself makes: plenty of golf brands have dabbled in camo without much of it meaning anything.

artisan.name: Artisan Golf · Est. 2017
artisan.desc: Mike Taylor and John Hatfield came off the Nike payroll on a Friday in February 2017 and opened Artisan the following Monday, in the same ten-thousand-square-foot shop Nike had used to build golf clubs. Taylor was Nike’s model maker for irons and wedges and Hatfield built putters. Taylor still grinds every wedge himself, and you cannot order one without coming to Fort Worth to be fitted.

p53.name: P53 Irons · Founded by Christopher Griffin
p53.desc: Christopher Griffin left Microsoft in 2012 to build P53, named for Ben Hogan’s 1953 season, the year he won three of the four. The shop leases space at Leonard Golf Links — the old Nike building — from Marty Leonard, whose father founded Colonial. Every iron starts as a single billet of certified American steel, struck at around 2,100°F under a gravity hammer, then machined, ground and finished in house. Admission is by invitation only.

piretti.name: Piretti Putters · Est. 2008
piretti.desc: Mike Johnson designs every Piretti head, and every one is milled from a solid billet — there has never been a cast putter in the line. Two specs set him against the rest of the industry: heads run fifteen to forty-five grams heavier than standard, and loft is set at 2.5 degrees because greens are cut shorter than they used to be. It is all made in a shop on Stuebner Airline Road north of Houston.

edison.name: Edison Golf · Est. 2018
edison.desc: Terry Koehler has been designing wedges longer than most brands have existed: EIDOLON, which put the first CNC-milled grooves in a production wedge, then SCOR, then the Ben Hogan relaunch. Edison is the distillation of all of it, and the patented Koehler Sole puts high and low bounce in the same head so one wedge covers more lies. In 2021 he moved design, assembly and shipping to the Gulf Coast at Rockport.

The Brick is milled in the USA from premium stainless and hand-finished in Austin; the E-T01 is machined from carbon steel, then hand-painted, polished and assembled in Austin. Each head is finished individually by their own craftsmen.

Their own description is the least romantic and the most accurate: a family owned Texas based machine shop. Putters are the headline and the engraving is the signature, turning up on ball markers, divot tools and the leather.

3.html: That last one is the closest thing to a pattern. P53 leases its space in that same building from Marty Leonard, whose father Marvin built Colonial. Ben Hogan is buried in the city. The metal work clusters where it does for a reason.

manors.name: Lightweight Course Trousers 2.0

The softer, roomier Club Pant is the sibling, but that one only comes in Earth, Pine Green and Vapour. Black lives here.

odd-ritual.name: Classic Polo

metalwood.name: Quarter Zip Jersey Polo

devereux.name: Phoenician Polo
devereux.desc: Devereux runs the Phoenician in a textured knit with a johnny collar, a patch pocket, and its only branding tucked into a woven label at the neck. The texture is the reason to buy it. Flat black jersey goes shiny and cheap in direct sun, while a knit with this much surface catches shadow and holds its depth all the way through a round.
devereux.old: Textured knit, johnny collar, patch pocket, and a woven neck label doing all the branding. The texture is what makes it — flat black jersey reads cheap under sun, and a knit like this holds shadow instead of shine.

criquet.name: Retro Coach’s Players Shirt
criquet.desc: Criquet is an Austin shop with a long obsession with mid-century clubhouse clothing, and the Retro Coach’s barely reads as golf at all. It is a camp-collar popover with a flap pocket on the chest and no visible logo anywhere on it. Wear it straight to dinner afterward and nobody has to know you played thirty-six.
criquet.old: The Austin entry, and the least golf-looking garment in the post. Camp-collar popover with a chest flap pocket and no visible logo at all. Wears to dinner without anyone clocking that you played thirty-six.

left-of-field.name: Stanwell Pleated Wide Trouser
left-of-field.desc: Left of Field cuts the Stanwell with a double pleat and the widest leg in golf, which puts it closer to a 1950s trouser than to anything hanging in a pro shop. There is no branding on the front at all. It breaks properly over a shoe instead of stopping short at the ankle, and it is the pant for the round where you are mostly drinking.
left-of-field.old: The dressier counterweight to the Manors pant, and the widest leg you will find in golf. Pleated, no front branding, cut to break properly over a shoe. If the Manors trouser is for playing, this one is for the nine holes where you are mostly drinking.

malbon.name: Studio Seoul Piste Crewneck
malbon.desc: Studio Seoul is where Malbon keeps its restraint, and the Piste Crewneck is cut from a technical piste fabric with a single embroidered mascot patch doing all the branding. It runs a full size range. This is the most expensive layer here and the one that will read least like golf on the walk in from the car.
malbon.old: Technical piste fabric with a small embroidered mascot patch, which for Malbon counts as restraint. Full size run. The most expensive layer here and the one that will look least like golf on the walk from the car.

random-golf-club.name: City Golf Hoodie
random-golf-club.desc: Random Golf Club makes this in a true black fleece with a small centred wordmark and charges seventy-five dollars for it. Every blacked-out kit needs one layer you are not precious about — the one that lives in the boot of the car from October onward and comes out smelling faintly of range balls.
random-golf-club.old: True black fleece, small centred wordmark, and seventy-five dollars. Every blacked-out kit needs one piece you do not care about, and this is it — the layer that lives in the boot of the car from October onwards.

fella.name: Fella Logo Tee
fella.desc: Fella cuts this boxy in a heavyweight cotton that hangs off the shoulder instead of clinging, with one small script logo on the chest and a clean back. Most golf tees are ruined by the graphic. This one is built to sit under a quarter-zip and stay out of the way.
fella.old: The plain black tee, done properly. Heavyweight cotton, boxy cut, one small script logo on the chest and nothing on the back. The whole category is usually ruined by a graphic; this is the one that just gets out of the way.

merrill.name: Golf Company LS Tee
merrill.desc: Merrill Golf Company makes the long-sleeve answer to shoulder season, or to anyone who has had the conversation with a dermatologist. It carries a small collegiate wordmark on the chest and, unusually for a vintage-leaning tee, holds a true black rather than the washed grey most of them settle into after a season.
merrill.old: The long-sleeve version, for shoulder season and for anyone who has been told about sun damage. Small collegiate wordmark on the chest, true black rather than the washed grey most vintage-styled tees end up as.

penta.name: Hazard Shorts
penta.desc: Penta builds the Hazard in nylon with an integrated belt and a subtle wordmark on the mesh pocket. It holds a real black in daylight rather than the charcoal most technical shorts turn out to be, and the cut sits mid-thigh with enough room through the seat to walk eighteen in.
penta.old: The only shorts that survived the colour test. Nylon, belted, with a subtle wordmark on the mesh pocket. Everything else in the category turned out to be charcoal wearing a black name.

duca-del-cosma.name: Grado
duca-del-cosma.desc: Duca del Cosma is a Dutch house that makes its shoes in Italy, which is why the Grado reads less like golf footwear and more like something you would keep on for dinner. Spikeless, waterproof, built on a chunky lugged sole with real streetwear proportions, and rendered in one uninterrupted black from upper to outsole. Golf Monthly gave it an Editor’s Choice.
duca-del-cosma.old: Solid black spikeless, waterproof, sizes seven to thirteen. Golf Monthly gave it an Editor's Choice. It is also the only shoe in golf we could find that is black all the way through — no contrast sole, no white midsole stripe, no orange heel counter. That sounds like a low bar. It is not.

mogshade.name: Dogleg Socks, Black
mogshade.desc: Mogshade is Portuguese and usually works in loud azulejo tile prints, so the plain black Dogleg is the quiet exception in its own range. The knit has a ribbed cuff that holds its shape through a wash cycle and a small logo at the ankle, and it sits low enough that nothing announces itself above the shoe line.
mogshade.old: The only black sock in independent golf, and we did look. Inside Story's entire twenty-three-item catalogue is ivory, white, royal blue, berry and cream. Mogshade is Portuguese, usually works in loud azulejo tile prints, and made exactly one thing that fits this post.

jones.name: Original Bomber, Black Vinyl
jones.desc: Jones Sports Co has been making this shape since 1971 and the Original Bomber is still unstructured — no legs, no cart strap, no panelling to break up the surface. In solid black vinyl it disappears entirely behind whatever you are wearing. This is a bag for people who walk, carry, and do not need it to say anything on their behalf.
jones.old: Unstructured, no legs, no cart strap, nothing. Solid black vinyl with no panelling. Jones has been making this shape since 1971 and the black one is the version that disappears entirely behind whatever you are wearing.

seamus.name: Black Suede Leather Driver
seamus.desc: Seamus built its name on Pendleton tartan, which makes the all-black suede driver cover the outlier in its own catalogue. Suede outside, black fleece lining inside, no printed graphic anywhere on it. This is the version they make for people who would rather not have the pattern conversation on the first tee.
seamus.old: Black suede outside, black fleece lining inside, zero printed graphics. Seamus built its name on Pendleton tartan, so the all-black suede is the outlier in their own range — the one they make for people who do not want the pattern conversation.

clint-orms.name: 1″ Tapered Black Ostrich
clint-orms.desc: Clint Orms is a Texas silversmith better known for hand-engraved buckles, which makes a plain strap the sleeper in his catalogue. This one is full-quill ostrich, tapered to an inch, carrying the raised follicle texture that flat dyed calf never has. The snap closures mean you can put one of his buckles on it later and undo all this restraint.
clint-orms.old: Clint Orms is a Texas silversmith better known for engraved buckles, which makes the plain black ostrich strap the sleeper. Full-quill, so it has visible follicle texture rather than flat dyed calf. Snap closures, so you can put a buckle on it later and undo all this restraint.

huega-house.name: Icon Performance Hat
huega-house.desc: Huega House puts a structured crown on the Icon, and that is most of what separates a forty-nine dollar hat from a twenty dollar one. It holds its shape through a summer instead of collapsing at the front after two rounds. Clean black, no contrast stitching, and the brand’s best seller by a distance.
huega-house.old: Structured performance crown, clean black, their best seller. The shape holds rather than collapsing after two rounds, which is most of what separates a forty-nine dollar hat from a twenty dollar one.

devant.name: Tour Microfiber Towel
devant.desc: Devant has been making towels since 1976 and holds the licences for the USGA, the PGA of America, the PGA Tour and the LPGA, so the towels you watch on tour bags every Sunday come off this line. Solid black waffle weave with a centre hang slit, twenty dollars, and no logo on it at all.
devant.old: Twenty bucks, solid black waffle weave, centre hang slit. Devant has been making towels since 1976 and holds the licences for the USGA, the PGA of America, the PGA Tour and the LPGA, so this is the same towel as the ones on tour bags with the logos taken off.

piretti.name: Potenza Wide Body, Black Oxide
piretti.desc: Piretti milled the Potenza Wide Body from 11L17 carbon steel and finished it in black oxide, in a serialised run of one hundred, right hand only. Black oxide is a gunsmith’s finish rather than a paint, so it wears thin at the edges and around the sole over years of use. It ages like a tool instead of chipping like a coating.
piretti.old: The one piece of equipment, and the one splurge. Serialised run of one hundred, 11L17 carbon steel in a black oxide finish, right hand only. Black oxide is a gunsmith's finish rather than a paint — it will wear at the edges over years, which is the point.

1.label: Eleven · polos, tees, trousers, layers
1.text: The clothing covers both halves: two trousers cut for different jobs, three collars, two tees, a hoodie, and a pair of shorts that stays black in daylight instead of sliding to charcoal.
1.old: Two trousers because they solve different problems, three collars, two tees, and the shorts that survived. Everything here was checked against the product photo rather than the colourway name.

2.label: Two · shoes and socks
2.text: From the ankle down, golf almost always interrupts black with a contrast sole or a cream stripe through the midsole. Both of these hold one unbroken colour.
2.old: A short section, and not for lack of looking. Golf makes almost nothing black from the ankle down without a contrast sole or a cream stripe.

3.label: Three · bag, cover, belt
3.text: Hardware is where all-black usually falls apart — a red zip pull here, a chrome logo plate there, and the whole effect goes. These three hold the line.
3.old: The hardware, and the section that took the longest to fill. Blacked-out bags are usually let down by one red zip pull, and blacked-out leather is usually just very dark brown.

4.label: Three · cap, towel, putter
4.text: This section runs from a twenty dollar towel to a thousand dollar putter, with a cap in between that holds its shape far longer than its price suggests. All three are finishing pieces.
4.old: The last twenty dollars and the first thousand. One of these is the cheapest thing in the post and one is the most expensive, and they are both doing the same job.

1.html: All-black is the easiest look in golf to describe and the hardest to assemble, because roughly half of what the industry sells as black is not black. It is charcoal, or gunmetal, or garment-washed to a soft grey, or a navy so deep it only shows itself next to the real thing. Put two of those together on a first tee and the effect collapses.
1.old: All-black is the easiest look in golf to describe and the hardest to actually assemble, because roughly half of what the industry sells as black is not black. It is charcoal, or gunmetal, or garment-washed to a soft grey, or a navy so deep it only reveals itself next to the real thing. Put two of those together on a first tee and the whole idea falls apart.

2.html: The colourway name is no guide to any of that. Brands sell charcoal as black and washed grey as black, and the gap stays invisible until the piece is on a body in daylight, next to something that actually is black.
2.old: So the rule for this one was simple and slightly tedious: open the product photo and look at it. Not the colourway name, not the filter, the actual picture. A lot of things did not survive that.

3.html: Near-black turns up all over the category. Siegelman’s black hoodies are vintage-dyed to a visible faded grey. Devereux’s Anorak is a black and graphite colourblock. Malbon’s jackets carry blue zips or white side panels. BestGrips sells a putter cover whose file name says black and whose photograph is unmistakably green. Royal Albartross makes handsome shoes and every men’s pair has a contrast sole, welt or heel counter. Artisan’s darkest putter finish is called Gunmetal, which is at least honest.
3.old: Siegelman’s black hoodies are vintage-dyed to a visible faded grey. Devereux’s Anorak is a black and graphite colourblock. Malbon’s jackets all have blue zips or white side panels. BestGrips sells a putter cover whose file name says black and whose photograph is unmistakably green. Royal Albartross makes handsome shoes and every single men’s pair has a contrast sole, welt or heel counter. Artisan’s darkest putter finish is called Gunmetal, which is at least honest.

4.html: What holds up is nineteen pieces, one per brand, head to toe — two trousers, three collars, two tees, a hoodie, shorts, shoes, socks, a bag, a headcover, a belt, a cap, a towel and one thousand-dollar putter. Gloves and socks are where the category thins out, so both slots came down to a single option each.
4.old: What is left is nineteen pieces, one per brand, head to toe — two trousers, three collars, two tees, a hoodie, shorts, shoes, socks, a bag, a headcover, a belt, a cap, a towel and one thousand-dollar putter. Two gaps we could not fill and will not pretend otherwise: nobody independent makes a black glove, and exactly one brand makes a black sock.

#1.name: Rory’s Masters Winning Marker (2025) · $115
#1.desc: Jon Millman hand stamps, torches and paints copper in Melville, New York, and this is his replica of the marker that completed the career Grand Slam at the 2025 Masters. The finish comes off a torch rather than a plating line, so no two discs land in the same place tonally. Golf Life Metals sells it at $115.
#1.old: The 2025 Masters marker, the one that completed the career Grand Slam.

#2.name: Rory’s Players Winning Marker (2025) · $115
#2.desc: The 2025 Players marker comes out of the same hands and the same copper as the Masters piece. Millman stamps, torches and paints every one in Melville, so a replica carries the same variation the original had. Golf Life Metals prices all of these at $115.
#2.old: Players Championship, 2025. Same hands, same copper.

#3.name: Tommy’s Tour Championship Winning Marker (2025) · $115
#3.desc: Tommy Fleetwood won the 2025 Tour Championship and Golf Life Metals sells the replica of the marker that went with him. The copper is stamped and torched by hand in a unit on Broadhollow Road, which is why the tone shifts from disc to disc. Millman charges $115.

#4.name: Darren Clarke’s Senior Open Winning Marker (2021) · $115
#4.desc: Darren Clarke had one of these in his pocket for the 2021 Senior Open, which puts the shop’s tour record back further than the recent run suggests. The build is the same hand-stamped, torch-finished copper Golf Life Metals sells across the catalogue at $115.
#4.old: Darren Clarke's 2021 Senior Open winner, and proof this is not a recent fluke.

#5.name: Shane Lowry’s Ryder Cup Marker · $115
#5.desc: Shane Lowry has a Ryder Cup piece in the Golf Life Metals catalogue, and the shop lists an official Ryder Cup marker alongside it. Both are hand-stamped copper at $115, torched and painted by hand in Melville rather than pressed and plated somewhere else.
#5.old: Lowry's Ryder Cup piece. GLM also lists an official Ryder Cup marker.

#6.name: Jack Nicklaus’ GLM Marker · $115
#6.desc: Golf Life Metals has made markers for Jack Nicklaus, and the shop’s own line is “we’ve made for Jack, Tiger, Scottie.” The Nicklaus design sells to anybody at $115, in the same torched copper Millman uses for the tour work.
#6.old: They made one for Jack. The site's line is “we've made for Jack, Tiger, Scottie.”

#7.name: Grand Slam Marker · $115
#7.desc: The Grand Slam design is the one Golf Life Metals sells to anybody, with no name attached to it. Millman stamps it into copper and finishes it with a torch the same way he does the tour replicas, at the same $115.
#7.old: The Grand Slam design, sold to anyone.

#8.name: US Open – Shinnecock · $115
#8.desc: Shinnecock gets the full treatment, torched copper with hand-painted numerals, which is where the shop’s technique shows most clearly. Paint sitting down in a stamped recess reads at arm’s length in a way an etched disc never does. Golf Life Metals charges $115.

#9.name: Fuck Bogeys · $115
#9.desc: Golf Life Metals sells this one out of the same catalogue as the Nicklaus marker, six inches down the same page. The build does not change either: hand-stamped copper, torch finish, $115. The shop draws no distinction between the two in price or in method.
#9.old: Sits in the same catalogue as the Nicklaus marker. That is the whole personality of the shop in one product listing.

#10.name: Copper Blanks · $6
#10.desc: The blanks are raw copper discs at six dollars, sold for anybody who would rather do the stamping themselves. Nothing is torched and nothing is painted, which is the point of buying the metal before Millman gets to it. Six dollars is the floor of the catalogue.
#10.old: Six dollars for a raw copper disc, if you would rather stamp your own.

#11.name: Rory’s Masters Winning Marker (2026) · $115
#11.desc: Golf Life Metals has “Rory’s Masters markers (both)” at the top of its homepage, meaning the 2025 piece and this one from 2026. The shop also hosts a video called Making Rory’s Grand Slam Marker if you want to watch the copper go under the torch. It sells for the same $115 as the rest.
#11.old: The 2026 one. GLM's homepage leads with “Rory's Masters markers (both)” and hosts a video called Making Rory's Grand Slam Marker.

#12.name: Hand Forged® Anvil Steel · $36
#12.desc: Seamus forges in Portland, striking every piece by hand so no two come out identical. This one is an anvil, struck on an anvil, in steel. At $36 it is about as literal as a maker’s mark gets.
#12.old: An anvil, struck on an anvil. Steel.

#13.name: Hand Forged® Sakura Ball Marker - Copper · $48
#13.desc: The Sakura is a cherry blossom forged into copper and the prettiest shape Seamus hammers out. Copper takes a patina faster than steel does, so the petals will darken down into the recesses over a season of being handled. Seamus prices it at $48.
#13.old: Cherry blossom in copper, and the prettiest thing Seamus forges.

#14.name: Hand Forged® Lucky Horseshoe Ball Marker - Steel · $48
#14.desc: The horseshoe is steel and sits in the $48 tier, which is where the more involved shapes live. Seamus forges each one by hand in Portland, so the curve and the nail holes land slightly differently every time.
#14.old: Steel horseshoe. The $48 tier is where the more involved shapes live.

#15.name: Hand Forged® Labyrinth Ball Marker - Copper · $36
#15.desc: The Labyrinth is a maze stamped into copper, and from a foot away it stops reading as a maze and starts reading as texture. That is a useful quality in an object that spends most of its life face down on a green. Seamus sells it at $36.
#15.old: A maze in copper. Reads as texture from a foot away.

#16.name: Hand Forged® Mesh Dimple Ball Marker - Steel · $36
#16.desc: The dimple pattern is forged into steel so the marker carries the same surface as the ball it stands in for. Seamus plays that straight, with nothing printed on it and nothing explaining it. The price is $36.
#16.old: Dimple pattern in steel, so the marker matches the ball.

#17.name: Hand Forged® Touch Gorse Bronze · $36
#17.desc: Touch Gorse is named for the stuff you will be visiting later in the round, forged in bronze at $36. Bronze is the warmest of the three metals Seamus works in and the one that sits between the copper and the steel.
#17.old: Named for the gorse you will be visiting later.

#18.name: Bronze Metal Hand Forged Fyfe Golf Ball marker · £25
#18.desc: Fyfe forges in Scotland and puts its house mark into bronze at £25. Hand striking means the edges and the depth of the stamp shift from one disc to the next, which is the argument for a forged marker over a printed one.
#18.old: Fyfe's house mark in bronze, hand forged in Scotland. £25.

#19.name: Copper Metal Hand Forged Fyfe Golf Ball marker · £25
#19.desc: The copper version costs the same £25 and takes a patina faster than the bronze does. It carries the same Fyfe house mark, forged by hand in Scotland, so the stamp lands at a slightly different depth on every disc that comes off the anvil.
#19.old: The copper version, which takes a patina faster.

#20.name: The Brave Copper Hand Forged · £25
#20.desc: The Brave is Fyfe’s other design, in copper at £25, hand forged in Scotland like the rest of the shop’s work. Copper is the metal that changes most in a pocket, so this is the one that will look least like it did on arrival.

#21.name: Old Tom Copper Marker · £25 · Sold out
#21.desc: Old Tom Morris goes into copper at Hame, in a £25 run that has now sold out. The shop works in small batches, so a sold-out marker there sits closer to a finished edition than to a restock problem.
#21.old: Old Tom Morris in copper from Hame. Sold out, and they make these in small runs.

#22.name: Truffle Shuffle · $20
#22.desc: Matchstick Golf has Chunk from The Goonies doing the truffle shuffle in enamel, on a golf course, for twenty dollars. The same catalogue holds a dinosaur caddie and three flavours of a Gatorade parody, and this is still the one that stops people. Nobody asked for it, and it remains the best thing the shop makes.
#22.old: Chunk from The Goonies, in enamel, on a golf course. Nobody asked for this and it is the best thing they make.

#23.name: VW Bus · $20
#23.desc: The VW bus is an orange split-screen in enamel at twenty dollars. Matchstick keeps its whole catalogue at that price, which is why the references can be this specific without anybody having to think hard about buying one.

#24.name: Teddy Roosevelt · $20
#24.desc: Teddy Roosevelt gets the enamel treatment, pince-nez and all, at twenty dollars. Matchstick draws its markers as small illustrations rather than logos, so a face still reads once it has been shrunk to the size of a coin.

#25.name: Chef Skull · $20
#25.desc: The Chef Skull is a skull in a toque over crossed bones, in enamel at twenty dollars. Matchstick runs a catalogue where that sits next to a president and a dinosaur and none of it needs explaining.
#25.old: Skull in a toque over crossed bones.

#26.name: Caddysaurus · $20
#26.desc: The Caddysaurus is a dinosaur carrying a bag, which is the entire idea and enough of one. Matchstick prices it at twenty dollars like everything else in the enamel line, and the drawing survives being shrunk to the size of a coin.

#27.name: Pirate Flag · $20
#27.desc: The pirate flag reads THE COAST across a Jolly Roger, in enamel at twenty dollars. Matchstick keeps the drawing simple enough that it still holds together at coin size. Twenty dollars is the flat price across the enamel line, whatever the reference.

#28.name: Josh Allen Buffalo Bills · $20
#28.desc: The Josh Allen marker is a Bills tribute drawn to look licensed without ever claiming to be, at twenty dollars. Matchstick draws these as illustrations rather than logos, which is how it gets within touching distance of a team mark. Buffalo will buy every one the shop makes.
#28.old: A licensed-looking Bills tribute. Buffalo will buy every one.

#29.name: Hand Forged® The Dude Ball Marker - Bronze · $36
#29.desc: Seamus forged The Dude into bronze at $36, which is a Big Lebowski reference rendered in metal instead of print. Hand striking gives the face a slightly different depth on every disc, and the bronze will dull down over a season.

#30.name: Hand Forged® Jack Nicklaus "Yes Sir!" Ball Marker - Bronze · $36
#30.desc: Seamus put the 1986 Nicklaus call into bronze, “Yes Sir!” stamped into a $36 disc. Forging it rather than printing it means the words sit below the surface and will still be legible long after the finish has gone dark.
#30.old: Nicklaus's “Yes Sir!” in bronze, the 1986 call rendered as an object.

#31.name: Majestic Iron Skull Marker · ¥10,125
#31.desc: MARK & LONA is a Japanese label and its skull marker is iron rather than the copper or bronze most of the category works in. At ¥10,125 it costs more than any marker outside the hand-forged copper tier, which is a lot of money for something you leave on a green.
#31.old: Japanese, iron, skull. ¥10,125, which makes it the most expensive marker here that is not custom copper.

#32.name: Coca-Cola Bottle · $14.95
#32.desc: Pins & Aces holds a real Coca-Cola licence, which is not what you expect from a golf accessory brand charging $14.95. The contour bottle is rendered correctly, curves and all, rather than approximated into a generic soda shape.
#32.old: An actual Coca-Cola licence on a $14.95 ball marker. The contour bottle, correctly rendered.

#33.name: Coca-Cola Bear · $14.95
#33.desc: The polar bear comes off the same Coca-Cola licence at the same $14.95. Pins & Aces has to treat the artwork the way a licensee does, so the bear is the bear rather than a lookalike drawn to stay out of trouble.

#34.name: Blazy Susan Silhoutte · $14.95
#34.desc: Blazy Susan makes pink rolling papers and Pins & Aces has a licence with them, which produced a co-branded golf ball marker at $14.95. The silhouette is the more restrained of the two designs, which is a relative statement.
#34.old: Blazy Susan makes pink rolling papers. This is a co-branded golf ball marker. Read that twice.

#35.name: Blazy Susan Smoke Pink · $14.95
#35.desc: The Smoke Pink version puts the colour front and centre at $14.95, on the same Blazy Susan licence. Pins & Aces runs two real trademark deals at once, which is two more than most of the category has managed.

#36.name: Tito's Splash Of Grape · $66.66
#36.desc: SWAG Golf has a Tito’s licence and prices the marker at $66.66, the house number the brand puts on nearly everything. Splash Of Grape is the louder of the two Tito’s designs and makes no attempt to hide what it is advertising.
#36.old: Tito's, $66.66, which is SWAG's house price and also a choice.

#37.name: Tito's Water Hazard · $66.66
#37.desc: The Water Hazard version runs the same $66.66 and the same Tito’s licence, with the joke moved from the glass to the pond. SWAG does not discount for a second colourway. Both designs come off a real trademark deal, which is uncommon at any price in the category.
#37.old: The water hazard variant. Same price, same joke.

#38.name: 2026 U.S. Women’s Open Riviera · $36
#38.desc: Riviera has the 2026 U.S. Women’s Open and Seamus forged the marker for it rather than printing one. The stamp goes into the metal, so it will still be there once the finish has worn off the high points. Seamus sells it at $36.
#38.old: Riviera, 2026 U.S. Women's Open. Forged, not printed.

#39.name: 2025 Ryder Cup Ball Marker - Bronze · $48
#39.desc: The 2025 Ryder Cup marker is bronze at $48, sitting in the tier where Seamus puts the more involved work. A forged commemorative ages differently to a printed one, which is most of the reason to pay this for a disc.

#40.name: Ocean Course QD Ball Markers · $19
#40.desc: Golf by QD is a Mexican brand that mostly makes caddie crowns, and the Ocean Course marker is the outlier in its catalogue. Kiawah lands at $19, which is a low price for a course that most brands would charge a premium to put on anything.
#40.old: Kiawah's Ocean Course, from a Mexican brand that mostly makes caddie crowns.

#41.name: Cleeve Hill · £5 · Sold out
#41.desc: Sounder comes from Cleeve Hill in Gloucestershire and named a marker after the course rather than after a tournament. At £5 it cost less than a pint, and the run sold out. The brand does the same thing with its bag towel.
#41.old: £5 for a marker named after Cleeve Hill in Gloucestershire, which is where Sounder is from.

#42.name: Cleeve Hill Northern Ball Markers Combo Tin · £65 · Sold out
#42.desc: The combo tin packages the same Cleeve Hill idea at £65, which is a different proposition to a single £5 disc. Sixty-five pounds buys a set in a tin rather than a marker in a bag, so it lands as a gift more than a purchase. Sounder sold through that one as well.
#42.old: The same idea in a £65 tin. Sold out.

#43.name: Azalea · $14.95 · Sold out
#43.desc: Azalea is a hole name that does not need explaining to anybody who watches golf in April. Pins & Aces made a marker out of it at $14.95 and the run sold out. Everything the brand makes sits at that price, tournament references included.

#44.name: 5280 · $14.95
#44.desc: 5280 is Denver’s elevation in feet and the shorthand the city uses for itself, which makes it a marker for people who play at altitude and like to mention it. Pins & Aces sells it at $14.95.
#44.old: Denver's elevation in feet, which is also a local shorthand.

#45.name: Liberty Bell · $14.95
#45.desc: The Liberty Bell marker is Philadelphia in enamel, crack included, at $14.95. Pins & Aces keeps its city markers to one obvious landmark each and leaves the rest alone. Every one of them costs the same $14.95, whatever the city.

#46.name: Putterade - Lemon-Lime · $20
#46.desc: Matchstick made three flavours of a Gatorade bottle relabelled as Putterade, of which lemon-lime is the one everybody pictures first. The shape sits close enough to the original that you read the bottle before you read the joke. Twenty dollars, in enamel, like the rest of the line.
#46.old: A Gatorade bottle relabelled Putterade. There are three flavours.

#47.name: Iced Coffee · $20
#47.desc: The iced coffee comes with a straw in it and a gold version alongside the standard one. Matchstick keeps both at twenty dollars, which is the price of every enamel marker the shop makes. The gold is the same drawing in a different finish.
#47.old: Iced coffee with a straw. There is a gold version too.

#48.name: Old Fashioned · $20
#48.desc: The Old Fashioned is a rocks glass with an orange peel and a cherry, drawn small enough to sit under a ball. Matchstick renders the drink rather than a brand, so nothing about it needs a licence, and the price stays at twenty dollars.

#49.name: Transfusion · $20
#49.desc: The Transfusion is the drink every muni sells and nobody outside golf has heard of, which makes it the most inside reference Matchstick has put on a disc. It sells for twenty dollars like everything else in the enamel line.
#49.old: The drink every muni sells and nobody outside golf has heard of.

#50.name: Flaming Coffee Mug · $20
#50.desc: The flaming coffee mug has a face on it and is on fire, which is a fair account of a seven-thirty tee time. Matchstick draws it in the same enamel as the rest of the drinks line and prices it at twenty dollars.
#50.old: A mug on fire with a face. For the front nine.

#51.name: Pizza Slice Double · €15
#51.desc: Fella Golf is a European brand selling in euros, and its pizza slice splits into two markers so a pair can share one purchase. The double format is unusual in a category that almost always sells singles. Fifteen euros.
#51.old: A slice, from a European brand, doubling as two markers.

#52.name: Red Party Cup · $14.95
#52.desc: The red Solo cup gets rendered in miniature at $14.95, which is a specific kind of American object to put on a green. Pins & Aces sells it next to the ice cubes and the two are made to be used together.
#52.old: The red Solo cup, in miniature.

#53.name: Ice Cubes · $14.95
#53.desc: The ice cubes are two cubes in enamel at $14.95, made to sit alongside the red cup. Pins & Aces builds most of its drinks line in pairs like this rather than as one-offs.
#53.old: Two ice cubes. Best paired with the one above.

#54.name: RWB Ice Pop · $66.66
#54.desc: SWAG Golf put a red, white and blue rocket pop on a marker and charged $66.66 for it, the same number the brand puts on nearly everything. The colours read from a distance, which is more than most markers manage.
#54.old: Red, white and blue rocket pop.

#55.name: Hand Forged® Pendleton® Sugar Skulls Ball Marker - Oil Can · $36
#55.desc: Seamus and Pendleton have a longer relationship than a marker suggests, since Pendleton supplies the wool for the Seamus towels. The sugar skulls come in an oil can finish, the darkest thing in the Seamus line and the one that hides the forging marks least. Seamus charges $36.
#55.old: Sugar skulls in oil can finish, done with Pendleton, who also supply the wool for their towels.

#56.name: QG x Seamus Hand Forged Steel Pennant Marker · $35 · Sold out
#56.desc: Quiet Golf sends the design and Seamus swings the hammer, which is how all three markers in the partnership were made. The pennant is steel at $35 and the run sold out. A collaboration piece gets the same Portland hand work as the house line.

#57.name: Limited Release Parmore x Posterlad "Go Golf' · £10
#57.desc: Parmore worked with the designer Posterlad on this one and came away with the cleanest graphic of any collaboration marker in the category. Ten pounds is a low price for a piece of actual design work rather than a logo scaled to fit.
#57.old: Parmore with the designer Posterlad. £10 and the cleanest graphic here.

#58.name: Northwood x RGC · $10 · Sold out
#58.desc: Random Golf Club and Northwood put both names on one disc and priced it at ten dollars. The run sold out. Ten dollars puts it at the bottom of the collaboration tier, where most of the other two-name markers sit closer to thirty-five.
#58.old: Random Golf Club with Northwood. Sold out.

#59.name: SHANGHAI BUCKETS BALL MARKER · $38
#59.desc: Malbon made this one for Shanghai Buckets, which marks a store rather than a tournament and tells you where the brand’s attention sits. Thirty-eight dollars puts it above the enamel tier and below the forged copper.
#59.old: Malbon's Shanghai Buckets, marking a store rather than a tournament.

#60.name: NIMBUS BUCKETS BALL MARKER · $38
#60.desc: The Nimbus version runs the same series at the same $38, another Malbon location getting a disc of its own. Buckets is the brand’s store programme, so these work as souvenirs of having been somewhere rather than of having played something.

#61.name: Hand Forged Panda Tiger Artists Edition · $36
#61.desc: Seamus forged an artist edition for Press Golf and the subject is a panda tiger, which is exactly as odd as it sounds. The forging is the same Portland hand work as the house line, at $36.
#61.old: Seamus forging an artist edition for Press Golf. Panda tiger, which is exactly as odd as it sounds.

#62.name: QG x Seamus Hand Forged Bronze Owl Marker · $35 · Sold out
#62.desc: The owl is bronze at $35, with Quiet Golf sending the design and Seamus doing the forging. It sold out, which is what happened to all three markers in that partnership, each of them priced the same and each in a different metal.
#62.old: An owl in bronze. Quiet Golf sends the design, Seamus swings the hammer. Sold out.

#63.name: QG x Seamus Hand Forged Copper Monogram Marker · $35 · Sold out
#63.desc: The monogram is copper at $35, the third piece from the same partnership and the plainest of them. Copper is the metal that moves most, so a monogram stamped into it will look older than it is inside a season. It sold out with the others.
#63.old: Copper monogram, same partnership, also gone.

#64.name: Winston Collection Tradition Leather Ball Markers · $18
#64.desc: Winston Collection makes its markers in leather instead of metal, and the Tradition is the tidier of the two finishes. Eighteen dollars buys something that will crease rather than patina, which is a different way for an object to record having been used.

#65.name: Ball Marker Crest 3 Pack - Black / Green / Brushed Gold · A$39.95
#65.desc: Walker Golf sells the crest in three finishes at once, black, green and brushed gold, for A$39.95 out of Australia. Three at a time is a different proposition to the single-disc impulse buy the rest of the category runs on.
#65.old: Three crests, black, green and brushed gold, from Australia.

#66.name: At The Turn Ball Mark Set · A$39.95
#66.desc: Birds of Condor built the At The Turn set around a hot dog, a beer and a pie in enamel. The set costs A$39.95 and is an accurate account of what actually gets bought at an Australian turn.
#66.old: A hot dog, a beer and a pie in enamel. Australian and accurate.

#67.name: Blockbusters Ball Mark Set · A$39.95
#67.desc: The Blockbusters set puts three film references into one A$39.95 pack, in the same format as the At The Turn markers. Birds of Condor sells its enamel in sets rather than singles, which is a rarer approach than it sounds.
#67.old: Three film references in a set.

#68.name: Winston Collection Pull-Up Leather Ball Markers · $18
#68.desc: The pull-up leather version costs the same $18 and ages the way a wallet does, lightening where it bends and darkening where it gets handled. Almost nobody else in the category works in leather at all.
#68.old: Pull-up leather rather than metal, so it ages like a wallet.

#69.name: Flame Magnetic Ball Marker Pin · $6
#69.desc: The flame pin costs six dollars and clips magnetically to a hat rather than sitting on a green. Matchstick uses the same drawing style it puts on the markers, shrunk down further. Six dollars matches a raw copper blank, which is the other thing at the bottom of the range.
#69.old: Six dollars for a magnetic flame pin. The cheapest thing on this page.

#70.name: Mystery Draw · $10
#70.desc: Ten dollars gets you whatever Matchstick decides to send, and the product photo is a question mark. Everything the shop makes in enamel sells at twenty, so the draw is a discount on the format as much as a gamble. It is a sensible way to move odd stock.
#70.old: Ten dollars and you get whatever they send. The product photo is a question mark.

#71.name: Flower Ball Marker - Silver/Sage | Left of Field Golf · A$10
#71.desc: Left of Field works out of Sydney and prices in Australian dollars, so A$10 is about as low as a designed marker goes. The flower comes in silver and sage, quieter than most things at that price.
#71.old: A$10, silver and sage, from Sydney.

#72.name: Script Ball Marker - Dark Green · A$7 · Sold out
#72.desc: The script marker sold out at A$7 in dark green, with the lettering doing all the work. Left of Field works out of Sydney and prices in Australian dollars, and it keeps the markers cheap enough that losing one in the rough costs nothing.
#72.old: A$7 script marker in dark green.

#73.name: Magnetic Coin Marker · $13 · Sold out
#73.desc: Eastside Golf sells a magnetic coin marker at $13 and this run has gone. The magnetic format means it lives on a hat clip rather than loose in a pocket with the tees, and thirteen dollars puts it under most of the enamel tier.

#74.name: Metal · $15
#74.desc: Vessel makes bags first and the marker follows the same logic, plain metal at $15 and made to disappear into a pocket of one. Nothing on it announces anything. Fifteen dollars is the going rate for a marker with no drawing on it.
#74.old: Fifteen dollars, plain metal, made to disappear into a Vessel bag.

#75.name: Ball Marker · £15 · Sold out
#75.desc: Casualist put an eight-point star with an eye at the centre on a £15 marker and sold through the run. The graphic sits closer to a tattoo flash sheet than to anything else in the category.
#75.old: An eight-point star with an eye at the centre. £15, sold out.

#76.name: BobRad · $15
#76.desc: Radmor calls this one the BobRad and prices it at $15. Fifteen dollars is the tier where most brands stop trying, and a plain disc at that price still does the only job a marker has.

#77.name: Golf Geek · A$19.95
#77.desc: GOLF GEEK sits inside a comic-book speech bubble on this one, in enamel at A$19.95. Birds of Condor is Australian and prices in Australian dollars, so the conversion works in your favour. The brand mostly sells its enamel in sets, and this is one of the singles.
#77.old: GOLF GEEK in a comic-book bubble. A$19.95.

1.html: A ball marker is the cheapest thing in golf that can still be properly made, and the best of them come out of a unit on Broadhollow Road in Melville, New York. Jon Millman hand stamps, torches and paints copper discs under the name Golf Life Metals, and his own storefront sells replicas of the markers that won the 2025 and 2026 Masters, the 2025 Players, the 2025 Tour Championship and the 2021 Senior Open. The site says the work has been in play at the Olympics and the Ryder Cup, claims more than fifteen hundred designs for fifty-plus tour pros, and puts it plainly: back to back Masters won with GLM. Six inches down the same page sits a marker that says Fuck Bogeys.
1.old: The marker to know about first comes out of a unit on Broadhollow Road in Melville, New York. Jon Millman hand stamps, torches and paints copper discs under the name Golf Life Metals, and his own storefront sells replicas of the markers that won the 2025 and 2026 Masters, the 2025 Players, the 2025 Tour Championship and the 2021 Senior Open. The site says the work has been in play at the Olympics and the Ryder Cup, claims more than fifteen hundred designs for fifty-plus tour pros, and puts it plainly: back to back Masters won with GLM. Six inches down the same page is a marker that says Fuck Bogeys.

2.html: The rest is a question of method. Seamus forges in Portland and Fyfe in Scotland, both striking metal by hand, so no two come out the same. Pins & Aces holds a real Coca-Cola licence and a second with a rolling-paper company. Matchstick draws its markers as illustrations rather than logos, which is how a dinosaur caddie and Chunk from The Goonies hold together at coin size. Sounder named two after a hill in Gloucestershire.
2.old: Below that the field splits. Seamus forges in Portland and Fyfe forges in Scotland, both striking metal by hand so nothing comes out twice. Pins & Aces holds a real Coca-Cola licence and another with a rolling-paper company. Matchstick has built a catalogue that includes Chunk from The Goonies, a dinosaur caddie and three flavours of a Gatorade parody. Sounder named two after a hill in Gloucestershire.

3.html: Seventy-seven markers from twenty brands sit in nine groups, running from hand-forged copper through licensed artwork to a line of drinks rendered in enamel. Prices go from six dollars to two hundred and fourteen, in five currencies, none of them converted, so every number is what the brand itself charges.
3.old: Seventy-seven markers are below, from twenty brands, sorted into nine categories that had to be invented because no existing ones fit. Prices run from six dollars to two hundred and fourteen, in five currencies, none of them converted. Everything is what the brand charges.

#1.name: Tropical Noir 1/1 ·  Ping s159 60° · Artist Series · $500
#1.desc: Show Out took a Ping s159 apart, laser-cut the head and put it back together as a single numbered piece. Tropical Noir exists once and sold once, which is what 1/1 means. At $500 it is the more expensive of the two Artist Series wedges.
#1.old: A Ping s159 taken apart, laser-cut and put back together as a single numbered piece. Sold out, which is what 1/1 means.

#2.name: THE WATCHER 1/1 ·  Titleist Vokey 56° · Artist Series · $450
#2.desc: THE WATCHER is the other Artist Series piece, engraved on a Titleist Vokey 56 and sold at $450. Vincent Newman works out of a unit in Gilbert, Arizona, and the shipping address on his own site is a house. That is the scale this whole tier operates at.
#2.old: The other Artist Series piece, on a Vokey 56. Vincent Newman works out of a unit in Gilbert, Arizona, and the shipping address on his own site is a house.

#3.name: Sparky &middot; Stencil Lab Edition · $150
#3.desc: Stencil Lab is the pre-set tier, a fixed design applied to the wedge you send in, and it costs less than a commission because nobody is drawing it from scratch. Show Out photograph these on engraving plates rather than on a club, so the plate is what you are looking at. Their line for the shop: serious about quality, casual about rules.

Show Out photograph these designs on engraving plates rather than on a club, so that is what you are looking at. Their line for it: serious about quality, casual about rules.

#4.name: Butch T. Cougar &middot; Stencil Lab Edition · $150
#4.desc: Show Out sell Butch T. Cougar as a pre-set at $150, a college mascot rendered in engraving. #5.name: Desert Diamondback &middot; Stencil Lab Edition · $135
#5.desc: Desert Diamondback is the cheapest way into Show Out at $135, and it is Arizona iconography from a shop that sits in Arizona. It is pictured as an engraving sample rather than a finished club, which is how the whole Stencil Lab range gets shown.

#6.name: Desert Drought Golf &middot; Stencil Lab Edition · $135
#6.desc: Desert Drought Golf is Phoenix humour at $135, in a state where the water conversation is not much of a joke. Show Out photograph it on a sample plate like the rest of the pre-set designs, so the club that ends up in your bag is the one you already own.
#6.old: Desert Drought. Phoenix humour, in a state where the water conversation is not really a joke. Also shown on a sample plate.

#7.desc: The commission route starts at $125 for entry-level engraving, runs to $250 for Signature and $375 for Complex, and ends with a club that exists once. #8.name: Lefty Love Lucky Wizard Texas Tea HLX 6.0 LH Wedge Set (52°, 56°, 60°) · $1000
#8.desc: Bettinardi built one left-handed three-wedge set in Texas Tea and put it in the Hive, which is the closest thing a major maker does to a one-off. Fifty-two, fifty-six and sixty degrees, $1000 for all three, and no second set behind it when this one goes.
#8.old: A left-handed three-wedge set in Texas Tea, one unit made. Bettinardi’s Hive drops are the closest thing a major maker does to a one-off.

#9.name: Lefty Love Zombee Black PVD HLX 6.0 LH Wedge Set (50°, 54°, 58°) · $1200
#9.desc: Zombee Black PVD is another single left-handed set, 50, 54 and 58 degrees at $1200. Black PVD on a left-handed set narrows the audience to almost nobody.
#9.old: Zombee Black PVD, also left-handed, also a single set. The names are not focus-grouped.

#10.name: Lefty Love Multi Bomb Steel Patina HLX 6.0 LH Wedge Set (52°, 56°, 60°) · $1100
#10.desc: Steel Patina is the finish that changes colour with use rather than holding its look, which makes it the odd one out among collector pieces. Bettinardi built one left-handed set at $1100, 52, 56 and 60 degrees. It will not look like the photograph a year from now.
#10.old: Steel Patina, meant to change colour with use rather than hold a finish.

#11.name: Limited Edition Nickel Chrome Blast Face 4 · $170
#11.desc: Indi puts the groove choice at checkout — conforming, or the non-conforming set they label Big Box Grooves and mark Not Tournament Approved. The nickel chrome Blast Face 4 is $170 with either. Choosing at the cart is the part that makes it custom, and the part that decides what you can enter it in.
#11.old: Indi lets you pick your grooves at checkout — conforming, or the non-conforming set they label Big Box Grooves and mark Not Tournament Approved.

#12.name: Limited Edition Bronze Blast Face 4 · $170
#12.desc: The bronze version of the same head is also $170, and bronze is the finish people choose when they want a wedge to look used quickly. Indi work out of Carlsbad, California, in a fitting studio they call the House of Spin, which tells you how seriously they take the sales floor.
#12.old: The bronze version of the same head. Carlsbad, California, out of a fitting studio they call the House of Spin.

#13.name: FLX Blast Face 4 · $170
#13.desc: FLX is the straighter leading edge, built for pickers and firm turf, and ATK is the other grind Indi offer. Same $170, same Blast Face head, and the decision is about how much ground you take rather than about how the club looks behind the ball.

#14.name: B.I.G. Bunker Beater · $129
#14.desc: Indi sell the B.I.G. Bunker Beater as a dedicated sand club at $129, well under half of what most wedges around it cost. A club built for one shot is an unfashionable idea, and at that price it does not have to earn a permanent slot in the bag.
#14.old: A dedicated sand club at well under half the price of everything around it.

#15.name: SPN V3 RAW FORGED WEDGES · $149
#15.desc: New Level forge the SPN V3 in raw 1020 carbon, which will rust, and sell it at $149 with a build configurator that runs to length in quarter-inch steps and about seventy shafts. They ship internationally and say so plainly, which is not the standard among makers at this end of the market.

#16.name: Desert Eclipse SPN Wedges (CLOSEOUT) · $100
#16.desc: Desert Eclipse is the previous SPN generation, on closeout at $100. New Level do not take returns on anything, because everything is built after you order it, and a closeout price does not change the policy. Order the loft and the length you actually play.
#16.old: The previous generation on closeout. New Level don’t take returns on anything, because everything is built when you order it.

#17.name: SMS Pro Wedge · $180
#17.desc: Edel charge one price across every loft, grind, bounce and weight-bias combination, so the SMS Pro is $180 whatever you build. The flip weight shifts mass to the heel or the toe depending on how you order it, which means two of these can sit differently behind the ball at the same spec.

#18.name: Custom Stick'em Wedge - Chrome · $199
#18.desc: The Stick’em is PXG’s configurable wedge, built to what you enter rather than pulled off a rack. Chrome is the $199 version and the cheaper of the two finishes. It is the most conventional-looking club in the range and the one that will date the slowest.

#19.name: Custom Stick'em Wedge - Black · $219
#19.desc: The black Stick’em is the same configurable wedge at $219, which is twenty dollars for the finish and nothing else. Black sits quieter behind the ball for anyone who finds chrome glare distracting at address, and it will wear through at the leading edge in the same time.
#19.old: The black version, twenty dollars more.

#20.name: Grindworks × Patrick Reed　BARRETT Wedge · ¥37,950
#20.desc: The BARRETT is the Patrick Reed signature wedge, priced in yen at ¥37,950 and sold at home in Japan. Outside Japan you go through a distributor, which is the arrangement for everything Grindworks make. It is the most expensive of their three wedges by a wide margin.
#20.old: The Reed signature wedge. Priced in yen and sold domestically — outside Japan you go through a distributor.

#21.name: 86 RAW Wedge · ¥27,500
#21.desc: The 86 RAW is SUS218 stainless, vibratory tumbled to a marbled raw finish, and it comes in four factory grinds at ¥27,500. Patrick Reed is credited with the spec. The finish is the reason to look at it, since a tumbled head reads mottled rather than uniform and keeps moving as the steel goes.
#21.old: SUS218 stainless, vibratory tumbled to that marbled raw finish, in four factory grinds. Patrick Reed is credited with the spec.

#22.name: ZIP Wedge · ¥20,020
#22.desc: The ZIP is the cheapest thing Grindworks make at ¥20,020, and it is still built to order after you buy it. That is the Grindworks position in one club. Nothing sits on a shelf waiting, whatever it costs, and the wait is the same at the bottom of the range as at the top.
#22.old: The cheapest thing Grindworks make, still built to order after purchase.

#23.name: FRZ Wedges Stock · $250
#23.desc: Fourteen sell the FRZ head two ways. Stock is $250 and ships as built; Forged Custom is made to order in about twenty business days and is non-returnable even unused. That second condition is stated plainly on their own pages, which is more than most makers manage.
#23.old: Fourteen sell the same head two ways: stock, or Forged Custom built to order in about twenty business days and non-returnable even unused.

#24.name: DJ-6 Wedges Stock · $220
#24.desc: Fourteen was founded in 1981 by Takamitsu Takebayashi, an accomplished amateur who started out designing clubs for other people’s brands. The DJ-6 is the $220 stock wedge in that line, and a company built by a designer-for-hire tends to know what a shape is supposed to do.

1.label: One Person, One Club at a Time.
1.text: Show Out works one club at a time, on a wedge you already own. You ship it, the head comes off the shaft, the design goes on, and it comes back numbered 1/1 because there is exactly one of each.
1.old: The smallest operations in this report and the only ones doing genuinely one-off work on a club you already own. You ship them a wedge, they take the head off the shaft, mark it, and send it back. Show Out numbers its Artist Series pieces 1/1 because there is exactly one of each. Vincent Newman runs it out of a unit in Gilbert, Arizona; the shipping address on his own site is a house.

2.label: The Configurator Tier.
2.text: Everything here is made after you order it, which is not the same thing as bespoke. You choose from a menu — grind, finish, loft, lie, length, shaft, ferrule — and you cannot ask for what is not on it.

3.label: Forging Houses and One-Cut Grinds.
3.text: Four Japanese makers have four different answers to whether you can actually buy one. Grindworks sells at home in yen and sends everyone else to a distributor. Miura is forged in Himeji, though the storefront you buy from is a US company in Scottsdale.
3.old: Four makers, four different answers to whether you can actually buy one. Grindworks sells at home in yen and sends everyone else to a distributor. 4.label: Fittings, Flights and Bank Transfers.
4.text: Artisan will hand-grind a wedge and stamp it however you like, but only after you fly to Texas and sit a half-day fitting. That is not a marketing posture; it is written plainly on their own site.

5.label: What They Will And Won’t Tell You
5.text: Every major maker runs a wedge personalisation program. Two of them publish what the limits actually are, and the rest hide the options behind a configurator that renders nothing until you are already inside it.

1.html: The wedge is the only club most golfers will ever have marked with their own name, and a small industry has grown up around that. It runs from a man in Gilbert, Arizona who takes the head off your Vokey so the shaft never sees heat, through Japanese forging houses that will hand-grind a sole to your attack angle, up to a Callaway employee in Carlsbad whose work sits in the bags of two former presidents and cannot be bought at any price.

2.html: It also runs through a lot of drop-down menus. Only a handful of these makers do one-off work: Show Out and the other independent engravers, Artisan in Fort Worth, KYOEI’s custom programme, and Anthony Taranto, whose wedges are not for sale. Grindworks, Fourteen, Bettinardi, Edel, New Level, Indi and Miura all label their wedges custom, and all of them mean built-to-order from a fixed set of options. Built-to-order is a good way to buy a wedge, but it is not bespoke, and the word custom covers both without telling you which one you are getting.

1.label: The Summer Default

1.html: It is August in Austin, which means the back nine happens at a hundred degrees and the only equipment decision that changes your afternoon is what sits on your head. So the run is built around that: rope crowns, mesh backs, perforated panels and full brims, from twenty-two brands, grouped by shape rather than by label.
1.old: It is August in Austin, which means the back nine happens at a hundred degrees and the only equipment decision that actually affects your afternoon is what is on your head. So this is a hat edit built for that specifically: rope crowns, mesh backs, perforated panels and full brims, from twenty-two brands we already follow.

2.html: What is not here is as deliberate as what is. No visors, because the top of your head is the part that burns. No beanies, for reasons that do not need explaining. No wool, corduroy or velvet either, all of which these same brands make and all of which can wait until November.
2.old: What is not here is as deliberate as what is. No visors, because the top of your head is the part that burns. No beanies, for reasons that should not need explaining. And no wool, corduroy or velvet, all of which these same brands make and all of which can wait until November.

3.html: Prices sit in the currency each brand actually charges, with nothing converted: pounds for Manors and Macade, Australian dollars for Gumtree and Birds of Condor, dollars for the rest. The spread runs from a thirty dollar mesh trucker up to a seventy-six dollar Siegelman, which is a narrower range than the shapes suggest.
3.old: The sweep behind this ran to 705 hats across 35 brands, 530 of them in stock. Everything below is live as of today, has at least three usable product photographs, and is priced in the currency the brand actually charges — pounds for Manors and Macade, Australian dollars for Gumtree and Birds of Condor, nothing converted.

1.label: Eleven Clubs, West to South
1.text: Barton Creek makes twelve, and it sits in its own section at the end as the only one of these you can realistically play. Every photograph here is the club’s own.
1.old: The twelfth, Barton Creek, gets its own section at the end — it is the only one on the list you can realistically play. Every photograph is the club's own.

1.html: Say you come into money, and not the comfortable sort — where in Austin do you actually go and play golf? The premise is slightly stupid, which is the best kind.
1.old: The premise is simple and slightly stupid, which is the best kind. You come into money. Not comfortable money — the other kind. Where in Austin do you go play golf?

2.html: Twelve private clubs sit in and around town and out into the Hill Country, and the architecture is better than most people expect. Coore and Crenshaw are here. So are Pete and Alice Dye, on Lake Austin, and Nicklaus twice, and Fazio. One of the twelve is the only golf course Jimmy Demaret ever designed, which happens to be the reason the senior tour exists. Another, as of last October, is David McLay Kidd’s first course in Texas.
2.old: We put twelve private clubs in and around town and out into the Hill Country against that question, and the answers turned out to be better than expected. Coore and Crenshaw. Pete and Alice Dye on Lake Austin. The only golf course Jimmy Demaret ever designed, which happens to be the reason the senior tour exists. Nicklaus twice. Fazio. And, as of last October, David McLay Kidd's first course in Texas.

3.html: What any of it costs is the harder question, and the answer is more interesting than a number.
3.old: Then we went looking for what any of it costs, and found something more interesting than a number.

4.html: The golf comes first, because that is the fun part. The door comes second, because that is the honest part of any private club.
4.old: So this runs in two halves. First the golf, because that is the fun part. Then the door, because that is the honest part.

1.html: Look at the bottom of a PAYNTR collab and you will find the partner’s name printed across the outsole. Not a logo on the tongue, not a hangtag. The tread. Turn over the Students shoe and STUDENTS reads through translucent rubber; the Forresters shoe says FORRESTERS across the same panel. It is a small decision and most of why these sell out, because the branding stays invisible until somebody is standing behind you on a tee box.

2.html: PAYNTR has now done twenty-five collaborations with eleven brands, and thirteen of them landed in the last seventy-two days. The previous twelve run across the nineteen months before that, so the pace has roughly quadrupled this summer, and most of what came out of it has already sold through.

The previous twelve are spread across the nineteen months before that, so the pace has roughly quadrupled this summer and nobody in the independent golf press has said so.

3.html: The brand comes from cricket. David Paynter played professionally, is the great-grandson of the England Ashes batsman Eddie Paynter, and started the label in 2017 because cricket footwear was bad. Golf came later, run out of Portland, Oregon with Mike Forsey and Michael Glancy Jr., who both had long careers in performance footwear before this. That background is why the shoes are competent and why the graphics live under them rather than on them.

PAYNTR’s own house line closes it out, and it is plainer than anything the brand makes with somebody else.
